speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MR. RAPP  NEWSPAPER ARTICLE RESPECTING APPOINTMENT AS CONSERVATIVE WHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of personal privilege having to do with a newspaper article written by Peter Newman which attacks me as the Tory whip supposedly appointed by my leader to the dismay of the caucus at large. The article also refers to my having ordered buses to take Conservative M.P.'s to Expo and reserving most of the seats for Diefenbaker loyalists.
This article is a fabricated lie. It attacks my leader and myself, and every Conservative knows it is a lie and would back up my statement. Peter Newman and I both came from Europe, his name originally being Peter Neuman. We know there was in Europe another who always fabricated lies. His name was Dr. Goebbels. Peter Newman has now taken on the role of Goebbels here in Canada.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)

subtopic: MR. RAPP  NEWSPAPER ARTICLE RESPECTING APPOINTMENT AS CONSERVATIVE WHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, also on a point of personal privilege in view of the fact that my name was mentioned in that article, I feel I should like to put on the record the fact that to the best of my knowledge there is no foundation whatever for certain inferences which have been drawn in regard to myself. It would appear to me from the wording of the article that there is an implication that I may not have been a
supporter of the leader of our party. I should like to go on record at this time as saying that I doubt very much whether there is anyone in Canada who is a greater supporter of our leader. I feel this way, Mr. Speaker, because I believe he is one of the greatest Canadians of our first century.
I also do not agree with the inferences which have been drawn about the whip of our party. I for one am heartily in agreement with the choice of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale as whip of the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted I should like to make a

May 18, 1987

The Address-Mr. Brown brief intervention in this debate, and my remarks will be very short. There are only four subjects I want to speak on, and I hope I will not be longer than an average of two minutes on each. The first subject is one of local concern and affects my constituency and neighbouring constituencies. The second refers to the province of Ontario, and the other subjects affect people living in all parts of Canada.
The first subject relates to the reception of C.B.C. television programs in Brantford and the surrounding area. There is a great need in my community for a relay station to be located between London and Toronto to facilitate the reception of these programs by the great number of people who live in my area.
The amount of money spent by the C.B.C. last year in respect of television was colossal, in fact something over $88 million. The people of Brantford pay plenty as their share of the cost of this venture, yet really cannot see the programs. If they can see them at all the reception is very poor. I live in the centre of Brantford, and I cannot see them at all. Some people may suggest that I move out, but that is something I will never do, particularly at this time of the year when the show of daffodils and tulips right in the centre of Brantford is such that I would not want to miss it.
Let me now refer for a minute or two to the operation of the general social welfare program adopted by this house and the Senate last year and made retroactive to April 1, 1966. I refer, of course, to the Canada Assistance Plan. More than a year later the Ontario legislature passed the family benefits act to make the Canada Assistance Plan operative in Ontario. What do we find in the province of Ontario more than a year after the Canada Assistance Plan came into effect? Nothing but chaos exists at local public welfare offices in this province since this legislation came into force. I do not wish to play politics in respect of the operation by the Ontario government of the family benefits act, but the people of this province will have something to say about this when the next provincial election is held.
This House of Commons did its best to make adequate provision for the blind, the disabled and the otherwise unemployed when this legislation was passed, and it was the wish of every member of this house that the people of Canada should benefit greatly from this legislation. These people are not receiving the results which each and every member who voted for the Canada Assistance Plan


last year expected, at least not the people in the province of Ontario.
This week I inquired about a disabled citizen whom I reported to the officials at Brantford nearly a year ago as one who required assistance. The officials replied just the other day that they were still waiting for word from Toronto as to whether this gentleman could qualify for assistance under the Ontario act, and no reference at all was made by those officials to the Canada Assistance Plan which was passed in good faith by this house. As a matter of fact I do not think they have ever heard about it. It was my feeling that I should advise this house how this legislation is being operated in Ontario. I believe at most two or three extra individuals would be required in my own city for the proper operation of this legislation. In other words I believe the Canada Assistance Plan is not being operated properly in Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I now come to my third subject, which relates to the pensions of veterans. These pensions were increased last year so far as the veterans were concerned but were not extended to veterans' dependants. I know the minister and his department are considering a change in this regard, as the minister has advised the house, but there is a great need for consideration at the ministerial level so far as an extension to these dependants is concerned. I am sure the minister will do something in this regard after the committee which is studying the matter brings down its report.
There is another matter in respect of veterans which puzzles me, and that is the fact
May 18. 1987
that veterans files are secret so far as the veterans are concerned. I think I know what 1 am talking about in this connection. When a veteran is admitted to a hospital everyone from the orderly to the physiotherapist can read the file, except the veteran himself. A file may contain secret information such as a report that the veteran has a personality problem, and everybody knows about this except the individual concerned. Surely these files should be made available to the veterans so they can read what the officials have said about them. I am sorry the Minister of Veterans Affairs is not in his seat at the moment, but I know he understands the problems of veterans and I urge him to act upon these matters to which I have referred in a way more favourable to the veterans, keeping in mind their personal rights as individuals.
I now come to my fourth subject. As a member of this house I wish to stress the seriousness of the housing situation. There is such a widespread need for housing that I think for at least the next two or three years we should have a special department to deal exclusively with this matter. I know the Minister of Labour who is vitally interested in the nation's business, himself feels there should be a minister dealing exclusively with the matter I have spoken about. As a matter of fact he said just the other day that a cabinet minister should be appointed who would devote his full time to Canada's housing problem, at least for the present.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In Brantford recently I attended a meeting of tenants of housing projects financed by the federal, provincial and municipal governments. I was very much impressed with the testimony of those tenants. They were all fine young men, some of them with many children to support. They stated that the monthly rentals they had to pay were too high, and I agreed with them. The rentals were fixed in accordance with the wages earned by the tenants and they went up sharply every time the tenants received a raise in wages, to such an extent that they were prevented from even attempting to purchase homes. In this way they were really discouraged from ever owning homes.
I believe this matter should be reviewed by the authorities. I attended this meeting as Brantford's member of parliament, and I am very glad I was present to meet and hear these tenants. Again I say housing should be the exclusive responsibility of one minister, and I intend to press for this from now on.
349
The Address-Hon. Martial Asselin
These are my points, Mr. Speaker. They may seem small and insignificant but they are all vital, and I intend to use what influence I have as a member of parliament to pursue them on behalf of my constituents.
In conclusion I should like to speak of the war in Viet Nam. I have little doubt that there is a strong feeling across Canada against the escalation of this war. I could become very much exercised over the prosecution and operation of this war by our good friend and neighbour the United States. There is only one thing which holds me back in this regard, and that is that in my opinion we can be thankful we happen to have as leader of the government a gentleman extremely skilful in the field of external affairs, a man of the highest moral calibre in whom the Canadian people can have the utmost confidence. I refer of course to the present Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
These are not idle remarks nor wishful thinking on my part. I say we can be thankful here in Canada that we have Mr. Pearson. He will never lead our nation astray among the nations of the world. We can have faith in him and in our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). I know we will continue to have faith in them both until these disturbing times are over and peace becomes firm and real.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night, before the house adjourned, I sought to explain to hon. members that it was urgent, in this centennial year, to revise our Canadian constitution.
This morning, I would like to conclude my contribution to this debate by saying a few words about this country's policy on Viet Nam.
Recently, Mr. Speaker, the secretary general of the United Nations dismayed the whole world when he predicted that the Viet Nam war was putting us on the brink of a third world war. Such an important statement by the chief of international diplomacy cannot be taken lightly.
When the secretary general of the United Nations accepted the renewal of his mandate, members of the general assembly of the United Nations promised him that he could count on their co-operation to bring an end to the war in Viet Nam and to restore peace in south-east Asia.

May 18, 1967

The Address-Hon. Martial Asselin
It seems to me that up to now, the secretary general has not received from the members of the United Nations all the co-operation he was promised. For some months, the United States have been escalating the war in Viet Nam with such atrocities that world opinion is now disturbed. True, measures must be taken to stop communist expansion in south-east Asia, but, I have never heard that force of arms could check ideas or a philosophy.
We are faced, Mr. Speaker, with an undeniable fact: the United States have gone into South Viet Nam and Washington is quite determined to pursue this war to final victory.
It seems that any political solution to the Vietnamese conflict has been set aside and a military settlement is being sought instead.
Bombings have caused heavy casualties among civilians and I shall refrain from describing all the atrocities committed on both sides since the beginning of that conflict. I think that the literature received by my colleagues in this connection speaks by itself.
It is not for me to pass judgment on the presence of the United States in South Viet Nam, but the United Nations charter provides specifically that every country has a right to self-determination and also has the right to have the government of its own choice.
Some will claim that the United States are there under international agreements whereby a country may ask another for assistance in case of aggression. However, without probing too deeply into all those reasons, I think we should look for the most useful means to put an end to that war which could have very harmful repercussions on a third world war.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has no definite policy about Viet Nam. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) have already said that they endorse the American policy about the Vietnamese conflict.
The government has also stated on many occasions that it was against the escalation and extension of the Viet Nam war. Canada hs also tried to apply with regard to that conflict a certain policy of neutrality; it has tried to act as an intermediary between the belligerents; it has even proposed compromise solutions to put an end to that war.
But, Mr. Speaker, we must now ask ourselves the following question: Could Canadian foreign policy concerning Viet Nam help end hostilities today? As we know, under military agreements, Canada is providing the United States with armaments which apparently are used in the Viet Nam conflict.


Recently, the Canadian members of the International Control Commission were publicly accused of supplying information concerning their mission to the American authorities. In this context, how can Canada be taken seriously by the government of North Viet Nam, when it proposes a political solution to end the conflict? How can North Viet Nam determine whether Canada makes its peace proposals in good faith when it knows that our country supplies arms to the United States which will be used in the fight against North Viet Nam?
It is obvious that our foreign policy is timid and uncertain, and Canadians certainly have the right to ask themselves questions, especially these last few days, knowing that the cabinet is divided on Canadian policy concerning Viet Nam.
[DOT] (12 noon)
I think all Canadians are interested in this Viet Nam question, Mr. Speaker. Last night a C.B.C. program called "Tirer au Clair" presented ten newspapermen who discussed Canada's position with respect to the conflict in Viet Nam. And, strange to say, these journalists who, in my opinion, were representing several thousands of Canadians, were almost unanimous to say that Canada should reconsider its policy concerning the Viet Nam war.
I think that the very fact that we witnessed recently, within the cabinet, divergence of opinions concerning our foreign policy should give the Prime Minister as well as the Secretary of State for External Affairs, cause for reflection and that both should consider revising their policy.
As I said earlier, regardless of cabinet solidarity, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) claims that Canada should dissociate itself from the United States concerning Viet Nam. The Registrar General of Canada (Mr. Turner) did the same, in a speech made in Montreal recently and, yesterday, the Prime Minister reaffirmed the policy of Canada with regard to Viet Nam, stating that no attention must be paid to the statements made by those two ministers and that only the statements of policy issued by himself and his Secretary of State for External Affairs must be considered.
That statement made by the Prime Minister, cannot satisfy us. All the people in Canada ask this government for a definite, clear and unequivocal statement on its policy conerning Viet Nam. First of all, our foreign
May 18, 1967

policy must be built upon that question so as to save the world from a third universal conflict and to ensure a lasting peace in southeast Asia.
For too long now, our foreign policy has only been a policy of mediation, without any originality. The time has come for Canada to show some maturity in that field and to make its views known without taking into consideration the opinions of Washington. Since our country was a member of the International Control Commission set up to supervise the implementation of the 1954 Geneva agreements, it had good reasons to assert its neutrality in the Viet Nam conflict, but it seems that this option was rejected and that Canada accepted Washington's invitation to provide a more or less symbolic contribution to military operations to fight aggression and infiltrations by North Viet Nam. Moreover, Mr. Paul Sau-riol of Le Devoir used those words in his editorial of May 16, 1967, I believe.
In my view, given the present circumstances, it is hard to envisage a solution of the Viet Nam war if we cannot convince the parties concerned that they must accept the good offices of the United Nations and especially of the secretary general in bringing together to the table of negotiations all the parties involved in this conflict. In my opinion, it is to that effect that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should make his proposals and offers of mediation exclusively to the United States and North Viet Nam.
Under the present circumstances, Mr. Speaker, Canada has no other possible choice in that conflict. Therefore, I appeal to the Prime Minister whose qualities as mediator have won him the Nobel prize for peace. The Prime Minister should have enough prestige,
I believe, to convince the United States and North Viet Nam that it is more than ever time to trust the United Nations and the secretary general in their efforts to restore peace in south-east Asia.
I wanted, Mr. Speaker, before concluding, to launch an urgent appeal to the Prime Minister of my country, in order that future generations may not accuse us of having failed to avoid a third world war.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate because I feel this is a most important year. This is the year of our Lord 1967, which is the one hundredth year since the institution of the confederation of the 27053-231

The Address-Mr. Flemming great country called Canada of which we are all so proud. I feel, therefore, a special urge to have something to say in connection with the speech from the throne which has been delivered to us by His Excellency.
Before proceeding with any remarks I want to congratulate the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) upon the fine speech he delivered in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like to congratulate, too, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote) upon the very fine speech he made. I have been here since 1960, and I do not believe I have ever heard any better speeches made in moving and seconding the address in reply. These speeches were most impressive. The mover especially, as I understood his remarks and his general attitude, indicated he was in complete control of the situation. He was very eloquent and very capable. He is a distinguished broadcaster by profession, and his broadcast to this house that afternoon enhanced his reputation.
I confess that I enjoyed his speech. At times when he expressed certain ideas in the course of his remarks I felt that he should have been speaking from this side of the house rather than from the other side, because he was advancing ideas which I consider are definitely Conservative doctrine. To give an illustration of what I mean I will paraphrase his remarks. He said Newfoundlanders had demonstrated that in order to gain the new it is not necessary to disregard or eliminate the old. New experiences can enrich an established and proud culture. He said Newfoundlanders continued to give loyalty to the land that made them but they were totally committed to the broader objectives to which we all aspire. He went on to suggest that the promise of confederation had been renewed and the wisdom of its founders vindicated.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I agree most enthusiastically with these words. I consider, however, that they could be condensed into two words if we wished to condense them. Those two words would be "One Canada". This would be the idea we could extract from the language of the mover, one Canada, and that is the national policy of the Conservative party. This is the policy that will stimulate and encourage the unity so important to us all. This is the policy that will make an already great Canada even much greater.
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Flemming [DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I believe, Mr. Speaker, located as we are in the northern part of the continent of North America, we should continue to make progress within the framework of this confederation called Canada. There should be no question about that at any time anywhere in this country. We should continue to be strong as one country, united as one people, diversified perhaps yet still united and speaking with one voice. Around the family conference table at meetings convened from time to time by the central government we should continue to advance our individual and provincial claims and aspirations; there is nothing wrong with that. At the same time we should be continuing to think at all times and in all places in the country of going ahead as one country and one Canada.
I believe I can safely say that in the year of our Lord 1867, 100 years ago, the province of New Brunswick was relatively well off. We were building wooden ships, and we built a lot of them. We had built the Marco Polo, the fastest ship in the world of that day. We were trading with the New England states of the United States, and were trading to our very great advantage. So we were not a weak colony at the time; we were a province which, considering our population, was comfortably well off.
After discussions and consultations with the representatives of the three other provinces New Brunswick was invited to become one of the founding provinces of the confederation called Canada. We decided we would join; we did join; we will continue to belong. It is our duty as a partner to continue an association which has now been enlarged from the four original partners in confederation to ten. The country has grown from colonial status to that of a nation. There is no such thing as turning back; no such idea exists in Canada today. We have put our hands to the plan and we should go ahead, and go ahead with great confidence in the future. We are committed to joint action with national objectives in mind.
The speeches made in connection with the motion presently before the house might very well be considered comments on the program the government has enunciated. As I said at the outset of my remarks I believe this year this debate is a little more than that. The fact that this is our centennial year is one reason to bring about a review of the past, an assessment of the present and a statement of objectives for the future. I think dealing with these three particular phases of our history, past,

present and future, might properly illustrate the opinion of members.
In dealing with the past I think we must bear in mind the progress that has been made by Canada as a nation. To start at the beginning, everyone will recall that the four provinces that agreed to the terms of confederation and made confederation possible went through a period of gradual development. History records that these were difficult years.
Professor Creighton in his book "Sir John A. Macdonald, the Old Chieftain", records many more interesting happenings. For example, there was the building of the Intercolonial railway linking the central part of this country with the maritime provinces, the link of that day which bound together the central part of Canada with the east. Then the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway subsequent to the entry of British Columbia into confederation was carried out according to commitments made to British Columbia when it entered confederation. This was the most important link of that day which bound together the central part of the country with the west.
This was no small undertaking, Mr. Speaker. Even today people who make the trip on the Canadian Pacific Railway through the rockies cannot help but be impressed with the magnitude of the task which must have been presented in those days. At that time the equipment we have today did not exist. There were no bulldozers or carryalls to move large quantities of earth. All they had were picks and shovels, horses and carts and some dynamite. These were the essentials of construction equipment of that day, and I marvel that they were able to find a pass through the rockies and put the railway through. It must have brought to the government of that day a tremendous satisfaction and stimulation in the knowledge that they were able to accomplish that which they set out to do, namely the building of a new and great nation.
And so it is today, Mr. Speaker, that confederation comprises ten provinces. One hundred years ago there were but four. After the turn of the century Canada entered world war I. The men of Canada who participated in that conflict covered themselves with glory, and the fame of this country spread around the world. Much sacrifice was entailed at that time, but those who fought in that war brought credit, honour and glory to this country.
Then 21 years later again came the call to arms. Canada once more responded, and
May 18. 1967

again great credit came to the country. Our fame and glory once more became known the world over. I have said before and I say again that it is the performance of our men and women in two world wars which has brought to Canada a great deal of the international prestige which as a country we have at this time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, 22 years after the close of world war II we are celebrating our centennial. We live in the northern half of the continent of North America which in area constitutes the second largest country in the world. We have made tremendous strides and now have over 20 million people, whereas 100 years ago we had only three and a half million people. This is great progress indeed, and we are on the threshold of even greater progress.
I believe the speech from the throne can be divided into two parts. The first part is a preamble dealing with the past; the second part is a summary of the government's proposed program. There are certain parts of the speech from the throne that particularly appeal to me. I am impressed with the place that the following paragraph in the speech from the throne, as reported at page 2 of Hansard, gives to the individual and to the development of the individual:
It was possible to think, in 1867, of the public responsibility primarily in terms of state responsibility. The new challenges, which we must and will meet, require the involvement of the whole society and the efforts of all our people. In this time of fast-changing dimensions, the central concern of Canadian society must be the well-being of each individual, so that, regardless of his place or station at birth, he will have an equal chance to realize his full potential in the economic, social, political and cultural sense.
A country is a home; it must be built and furnished for the good life of its people.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
With this part of the speech I agree completely. I believe all governments charged with the responsibility of presenting a program to parliament ought always to place the emphasis on those parts of the program that will contribute to the well-being of every Canadian. Nevertheless, as those of us who have had much experience in the past recall, what was done in the past by individuals was usually done with a desire to create conditions under which individuals could develop their talents and give full scope to their ambition, energy and desire for progress in an economic and social sense. By following that principle this country has progressed.
The Address-Mr. Flemming
I say to the government that progress will not continue to be made if handouts are promised to people without regard being paid for the need to produce. A government cannot keep adding people to its payroll, cannot compete with private industry for skilled and executive talent, cannot keep wasting money needlessly and recklessly, without running into deficit financing and being obliged, to avoid disaster, to borrow money to pay for current expenditures. Disaster will overtake us because we shall not be able to sell our goods in the markets of the world if those conditions I have mentioned prevail.
I listened with great interest yesterday to the speech of my hon. friend and colleague the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), who confirmed what we all know-though some do not admit this-that today people are worried about the reckless waste and extravagance of this government. Everywhere they look they see evidence of that.

The people are worried because that expenditure is causing the cost of living to increase. Every time they buy groceries or other necessities of life they see that the buying power of their dollar has dwindled. And the reason for this decline, as I said a few moments ago, is that so much is being paid for so little.

Groups of people are now doing work that was formerly undertaken by private industry. Money would be available for many more good things in this country if certain government operations were performed in conjunction with private industry, if private industry were asked to undertake certain matters, rather than harnessing groups of people who have been collected together because somebody wanted to build an empire, to perform them.

That is happening in this country, and I warn the government that unless that sort of thing ceases the country is heading for trouble and may be faced with disaster.
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Flemming
The people also are worried because they see money that is voted for crown corporations being disposed of by those corporations as they see fit, usually for useless or nonsensical purposes. Within the last hour we listened to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) talk about television. He said that on television alone the C.B.C. was spending $88 million. I ask, Mr. Speaker, where does that money come from? The answer is perfectly obvious. It comes from taxation, because it could come from nowhere else.
When the people of this country see that sort of thing I think in the first place they become discouraged; they wonder where all this will end. Second, they say "Well, if this is the way the government is throwing it away I might as well get all I can out of it." I am afraid that is the sort of reaction brought about by the situation I have referred to. I should be glad to go into more detail, but time does not allow me to do so.
Again I wish to refer particularly to those portions of the speech from the throne which refer to our natural resources, and to pollution. I might say I am inspired to quote what I am about to quote by the excellent speech made the day before yesterday by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Cantelon). He went into the subject thoroughly. What he spoke of as being an interprovincial problem in Saskatchewan in my province is approaching the proportions of an international problem. The difficulty in my province is that much worse. I quote from the speech from the throne:
The great natural resources that we take into our second century will be vital to us in meeting our needs and in maintaining our position as a major world trader.
That is what I said a few minutes ago:
Measures will be introduced by the government at the present session arising out of the need to conserve and preserve the great wealth with which Canada has been so richly endowed. Water itself is becoming a more and more valuable resource. Efforts to combat pollution are taking on an economic as well as a social significance and the federal government intends to press forward in cooperation with the provinces. In keeping with this objective, you will be asked to approve a new Canada water act which will provide a framework for the improvement and implementation of Canadian water policy.
I draw the attention of the house to the sentence "Efforts to combat pollution are taking on an economic as well as a social significance and the federal government intends to press forward in co-operation with the provinces." I am pleased to see that sentence, and I shall remark about it.
One of our greatest worries arises from the pollution of our water; and in New Brunswick, which is my native province, the problem of water pollution is most serious. We have eight large pulp and paper mills now operating, and another has been announced for the reasonably near future. We have mineral developments which are operating, and more are to come; also we have industries based on farm products. We need federal action because some of our pulp and paper mills are on interprovincial waters, some are on international waters, and we have a disposal problem. We need a regulating agency in which the federal government, with the provincial government, shall have a part. In other words the agency must have authority to act. As matters stand now the question always arises "Who has jurisdiction? Under whose jurisdiction does this matter come?" The house is indebted to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) who has spoken about water pollution time and time again.
New Brunswick has six good salmon rivers which must be protected and, where needed, improved. Those rivers should be preserved, for they are tremendously important to all New Brunswickers and to our tourists. We make tourists a business, yet we allow our waters to be polluted. We take no care of that which appeals to the tourists. Why do tourists come to our province? Because they want to get out of the cities. Canada at present has wide open spaces which attract the tourists.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
So I commend the government on this part of the speech from the throne, while urging them to do more than talk. It is not too late to effect an improvement, and it is not too late to clean up the mess. And there is a mess; I think this applies to nearly every province; I am not talking about New Brunswick alone, where I know there is a mess to be dealt with. The federal government must give leadership; it must co-operate with provincial and in some cases municipal authorities. The need is urgent, and action must be taken without delay. I hope no time will be lost before presenting something to this house which will set the machinery in motion for immediate action and subsequent improvement.
Having spoken in these general terms I wish to be more specific. At the present time we have a definite and pressing pollution problem affecting the Saint John river, one which is especially urgent on account of the large hydro-electric development 15 miles

May 18, 1967

north of Fredericton in central New Brunswick, where the dam across the river will be in operation by late 1967.
This will transform the Saint John river at that point and for a long way upstream into a virtual lake 55 miles long and as much as a mile wide in places. This water will not be fast running; indeed it will be stagnant for a portion of the time. It is clearly evident that a great effort must be made to keep such a large body of water free from pollution. Incidentally, something similar to a lake will be created by the building of this dam and will lie roughly parallel to the trans-Canada highway.
Having said this, and having asked the house to keep the need for action very much in mind, I wish to give some information relative to the Saint John river which will indicate the extraordinary difficulties of the situation and the need for special and immediate attention by the federal authority. The Saint John river rises in the state of Maine and flows a distance of approximately 50 miles or more entirely in that state of the United States until it becomes the international boundary between New Brunswick and the state of Maine beginning at St. Francis, Maine, and Clair, New Brunswick. It then flows a distance of something like 100 miles as the international boundary between New Brunswick and Maine until it reaches the town of Grand Falls in Victoria county.
Below Grand Falls and its mouth the river is all in New Brunswick, and it flows roughly parallel with the boundary for about another 100 miles until it reaches a point at or near the town of Woodstock, after which it swings to the southeast, away from the state of Maine boundary, and finally empties into the bay of Fundy at Saint John, New Brunswick.
It is hard to imagine any body of water having more difficulties of jurisdiction than has the Saint John river. In rough terms the river runs about one third of its course in Maine, about one third as an international boundary and the remaining third in the province of New Brunswick. I doubt whether a more difficult stretch of water could be found as far as jurisdiction is concerned.
The upper portion of the river, particularly the international portion, has town and villages on each side all the way down to Ed-munston. Edmundston is a city of over 10,000 people. On the opposite side of the river is Madawaska, Maine, another fair sized town. In Edmunston there is a very large pulp and

The Address-Mr. Flemming paper mill which dumps its waste into the river; in Madawaska, Maine, a finishing mill.
After leaving Grand Falls the river flows in a southerly direction and practically parallels the Maine boundary from Grand Falls to Woodstock, New Brunswick, a distance of approximately 100 miles. Within this distance on the western side of the Saint John river there are many fair sized rivers which empty into it after rising in the state of Maine.
There is the Aroostook river on which are located the towns of Fort Fairfield, Presque Isle, Caribou and Washburn, small rivers by the names of Big Presque Isle and Little Presque Isle and, finally, the Meduxnekeg river, upon which the large town of Houlton is located, flowing into the Saint John at Woodstock. Raw sewage, industrial waste from starch factories and waste from sugar beet processing plants are among the pollutants which eventually find their way into the Saint John river across which, as I have said, a power dam is to be built 50 miles below Woodstock, creating a 55 mile lake into which all the up-river pollution will flow. Is it any wonder that I am standing here and pleading with the federal government to do something about this situation because of the international implications involved?
I think at this point I should mention with much appreciation the tremendous effort which has been made by the mayor of Woodstock, Mr. Gerald Gallop, and the council of that town to secure co-operation from the state of Maine in improving the situation, and in pressing the provincial government to take all possible measures to improve the condition of the river in the New Brunswick portion of its course. They have worked ceaselessly and effectively to correct the situation to the extent of their ability to do so. But their authority is limited. The prestige of the federal government is needed. We need agents of the federal government who will step in and say "We represent the government of Canada. We are here to co-operate with the town of Woodstock. We are here to help them and to work with them and the provincial government in solving this problem." Incidentally, the authorities of Woodstock have had good results so far following their contacts with Senator Muskie from the state of Maine, and the response from a number of the town authorities in that state has been quite satisfactory.
My main point concerns the importance of finding someone who can speak for this nation with prestige and authority.
May 18, 1967

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I thank members of the house for their consent and assure them that my remarks will not be lengthy from now on.
The Woodstock Bugle, a weekly newspaper published in the town of Woodstock, also deserves special mention and appreciation for the campaign it has waged to inform the public of the seriousness of the situation and the need to press for all possible measures to effect an improvement. There has been a favourable response. I urge the government to initiate action in co-operation with the United States authorities to co-operate with the town of Woodstock and other towns up river in Carleton and Victoria. It may be said we should invite the International Joint Commission to pass on this whole situation and make it the subject of a study.
Mr. Speaker, we need something which will be more prompt and more effective than a study. This has already been studied to death. The question of pollution in this particular part of Canada has been studied again and again. Yet everyone who wishes to pass the buck says "We can do a study". These studies last for years. It is time action was taken. It is time to apply remedies. I believe the government should immediately send a member of the staff of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to the town of Woodstock to consult with the mayor and the town council, to ascertain what has already been done, agree on a further course of action, and then pursue it.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Having agreed on a course of action, and ignoring jurisdictional difficulties, they should bring back a report, they should recommend something to be done about this. Then the appropriate federal department, I presume the Department of External Affairs, could get busy and the provincial government could likewise get busy, and the state of Maine and the federal government of the United States would co-operate. There has never been any lack of co-operation in that respect. I think we are in a little better situation than that referred to by the hon. member for Kindersley

(Mr. Cantelon) yesterday, who said they were getting no co-operation. We are getting lots of evidence of a desire to co-operate, but there is no overriding authority under which the various bodies can co-ordinate their efforts and effect an improvement.
I believe the situation should be brought under control before the Mactaquac dam goes in this fall and the river becomes a 50 mile lake at this point. Therefore I appeal to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to give this matter immediate attention and provide immediate action. I appeal to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to deal with the matter in the light of the information I hope he will receive in such a report and in co-operation with the federal government of the United States of America.
I must say in all seriousness that the usual procedure is just not good enough in this particular instance. We are now well along in May, and I understand that the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission expects to have power from the Mactaquac development project by Christmas of this year. This means that the river will probably be dammed up in September or October. Therefore there is no time to be lost. Action must be taken immediately, and I appeal to the minister to lose no time.
So, in summary, I urge the minister with all the force at my command, and all the force I am able to convey, to secure immediately a report relative to the pollution situation on the Saint John river in New Brunswick. There are other rivers in the same province which require attention, but I believe it is quite appropriate to say that the Saint John river is the most urgent problem at this particular time.

Mr. Speaker, in participating in this throne speech debate I wish to raise a problem which we have tried to raise with only relative success over the last four or five years. That, of course, is the problem which confronts our people in Canada because of the housing shortage that we face, which is daily growing more critical.
I know that every time we raise this question we are accused by the government of making political capital out of it, and perhaps to some extent that charge is justified; but in a way that is our job, to raise these issues and to attempt to pressure the government as much as possible in order to have it take action. I think the record should show that there is not a single solitary minister in the
May 18, 1967

house at the present time when we want to discuss matters of this kind.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when one examines the whole housing problem as it confronts us here in Canada, in a way one almost despairs of ever being able to move the government or to make any impression on it which will steer it on to greater action. Every session we go through the same charade, when we place all the dreary facts on the record and nothing ever happens. When I was coming down to the house today to speak I picked up a speech I delivered four years ago, and I could bring it in and read it into the record verbatim because nothing has happened since and nothing has changed. So we will go through it again and hope something will happen, and that the government will take some concrete action.
I read the speech delivered by the minister in this debate and I could not believe my eyes. It was one of the most pathetic, inadequate, incomprehensible attempts to deal with the housing crisis that one could possibly have imagined. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, if you examine the record and look at the facts you will find that after 40 years the situation in Canada is that people in 1929 were actually able to buy better housing with a lower percentage of their income than they are in 1967.
That is the devastating comment that I make upon the history of North America's and Canada's attempts to house our people. We are actually further behind than we were 40 years ago. What are the dreary facts? Some of them should be placed on the record.
Fact: 100,000 Canadians are living in absolutely appalling conditions.
Fact: 20 per cent of all our dwellings have primitive bathing facilities and toilet facilities.
Fact: one out of every three Canadian homes is in bad condition.
Fact: we have a shortage of half a million houses just to catch up with the backlog of the last war.
Fact: half a million Canadians are living in substandard homes.
Fact: the economic council says we need a minimum of 170,000 homes every year from now until 1970, and 200,000 from that point on. We have never come close to achieving that target.
Fact: because of the housing shortage rents are going up 20 per cent each year and more and more of our people are being gouged.
The Address-Mr. Reid Scott
Fact: Canadian consumers spend more of their income per annum on housing than consumers in any other industrialized country in North America or western Europe.
Fact: a world survey shows us sixteenth among the countries of the industrialized world in terms of what we have to spend for housing.
Mr. Speaker, one could go on and on and on. Those of us who are interested in this subject have files five feet high indicating and documenting the total inadequacy of the attempts of the various levels of government in Canada to solve the housing problem. In my own city of Toronto we are in need of a minimum of 40,000 new homes a year, and we are building 21,000.
The cost of homes in Toronto is up in the stratosphere with the astronauts. In 1964 the average cost of a home was $19,000. In 1966 it had risen to $27,000 and today, 1967, the average home being sold in metropolitan Toronto costs $30,000. That, Mr. Speaker, is totally beyond the capacity of the vast majority of our people. That is why we on this side of the house get so annoyed when the minister gets up and mouths statistics about the number of housing starts and the amounts of money he is putting into the mortgage market, because all he is really doing is permitting people to build homes that 85 per cent of our people cannot afford to buy anyway. There is no percentage in such a proposition.
It is futile to say we have a housing crisis in Canada. To make such a statement is trite. It is perfectly obvious. It is the solution that is much more difficult, and that is where we are having our major problem here in the House of Commons. If you review the activities of the government in this year I think the first thing you have to conclude is that the present minister has to be removed. He is a fine person individually and nobody has any quarrel with his personal qualifications, but it is perfectly clear from his public utterances that he understands nothing about housing and is not prepared to assume any responsibility whatsoever.
For example, on January 25 the Toronto Daily Star reported a speech he made as follows:
Federal Minister J. R. Nicholson said last night said the housing crisis is a problem for provinces and municipalities to solve, not the federal government.
If the minister starts out with that type of attitude there is no hope at all of our ever solving the housing crisis. I know there are great constitutional difficulties in this field,
May 18, 1867

The Address-Mr. Reid Scott but to me it is fantastic that the federal government takes the position that we do not have a responsibility in this field. Housing is something that affects every Canadian from coast to coast, and every Canadian in every age group. It affects our young people who are getting married. The tragedy today is that most young couples getting married will never be able to own homes as long as they live because the costs are too fantastic and are going up all the time. It affects out old people who, because of our crazy tax system, are losing their homes because they cannot afford to maintain them. It affects the man with a family who is paying so much to buy or rent a home that he is depriving his family of all the other social amenities that are required for their well-being.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Yet the government sits here in Ottawa and takes the position that this is not a responsibility of the federal government. To me this is incomprehensible and fantastic, particularly when the department is headed by a minister who takes the view that this is so and all we have to do is vote money for mortgages, which permits builders to build homes that people cannot afford to buy anyway. I think it is absolutely desirable now, unfortunately, that the present minister be removed and someone put in his place who is prepared to give leadership and assume responsibility.
I remember that four years ago when the minister took over this portfolio we were congratulating him and saying how much we admired the opportunity he had, that he had it within his grasp to sort of paint the broad sketch for Canada and to really build for himself political epitaph by initiating and inaugurating a great new, imaginative housing scheme for our country. And he has done nothing. Unfortunately he will be remembered as a minister who did not accomplish anything substantial in this whole field.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but because of the complexities involved-and no one denies this; we know there are constitutional difficulties, that it is hard to come to grips with our provinces and the prejudices of our municipalities-it seems to me we need, as we have been asking for years, at least a full time minister. We have a part time minister of housing in Canada now; most of his time is occupied by the problems of labour, which probably accounts for the fact that nothing very much has happened in the field of housing. We have been requesting for years that if we are to deal with this problem adequately we should at least have a full time minister.

It seems to me that even if we had a full time minister he could spend the next five years doing nothing but trying to come to grips with this tremendous crisis that we face.
We sit here and quote statistics and figures, forgetting that people are involved. Old people, young people, citizens from coast to coast are involved in this question. It makes one ashamed to tour one's constituency and see the conditions under which so many of our people are condemned to live. I wish the minister would get off the cloud that surrounds him at C.M.H.C., where they feed him all these cooked-up statistics that he brings to the house, and would get out and see the conditions under which Canadians are forced to live. If the minister did this I think we might then get some sort of action.
I believe also we have to admit to the Canadian public that there is a crisis. This government have never even admitted that fact. They stand up in this house and tell us there is no problem and everything is rolling along well. I think once in a while we ought to be honest with the public and admit that there is a tremendous problem in this area, and there is not any easy or quick solution to it. We should admit that it will take the ingenuity and talents of people in the House of Commons, in our provinces and our municipalities for as long as we can foresee in order to come to grips with this particular problem.
One of the difficulties we face is the traditional constitutional prejudice of our provinces, which feel that any activity in Ottawa is an intrusion into their fields of jurisdiction. Surely this is something we have to fight against. I remember that when I used to be a member of a provincial parliament at Queen's Park in Toronto, every time a problem was raised I was told it was up to the federal government to deal with it. Now I am here listening to the federal government, and they say it is up to the province. Each side seems to spend its time hiding behind the British North America Act and shoving off the responsibility to somebody else.
If we do not accept some leadership in this area future generations will curse this parliament, because the whole housing crisis epitomizes the great dilemma of our generation, which is the urbanization of Canada, the flow of people to the cities and the increasing trend away from rural communities. By 1970 probably 80 per cent or 85 per cent of our people will be living in the cities. This creates tremendous problems for legislators, not just
May 18, 1967

in the field of housing, although that is more immediate and obvious, but in every conceivable area-education, culture, communications, transportation and revitalizing of the cities. This is the great problem with which North America will have to grapple over the next few decades. That is why it is frustrating to us in opposition to see a federal government that is not prepared to assume any responsibility at all, that takes the view that it can write off this whole problem, pass it over to the provinces and not give any real leadership or action.
Who is taking this attitude? It is the great Liberal party, the so-called party of progress, the new people, the young people, the ones who are going to lead Canada into the great new community. These are the ones who run around the country telling everybody that they are familiar with all the questions and know all the answers, yet when we raise a question of tremendous importance we are told it is not their responsibility and is not their sphere of activity. As I said earlier, if they continue in this way I believe future parliaments will curse us for having sat back and permitted this tremendous social problem to continue without attention, without leadership and without action.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment I was outlining the very critical housing crisis which faces Canada, and in the first part of my remarks I indicated that one of the major roadblocks was the minister himself. I know he will not take that comment in any personal way, but in view of his negative attitude and many responsibilities as Minister of Labour it is obvious to everyone that he cannot possibly attack this problem in any real way.
It is trite to suggest that we have a housing crisis in Canada. The solution to the problem is the difficult thing. We must find some way to come to grips with it and to make concrete suggestions as to what we ought to be doing. In the 15 minutes left at my disposal I should like to make an attempt in this regard, but hon. members will understand that in 15 minutes one could not possibly outline in any detail a complex attack upon a complex problem.
27053-24 j

The Address-Mr. Reid Scott
There are some things we can do in both the short and long range categories. In the short range we should start by tearing up the National Housing Act. I prefer to call it the national hoaxing act because it was designed over 20 years ago under conditions that no longer exist and in circumstances that no longer prevail. It was designed as the working man's housing act, but in these days one cannot qualify to buy a house unless one earns $8,000 to $8,500 or more per year. This is nothing but socialism for the rich and de-prival for the poor, and it is totally out of touch with today's circumstances. We must begin again by rewriting the National Housing Act.
Second, we must try to do something about the prices of homes. This is not going to be a simple problem because so many complex ingredients go into our houses. However, there are many things that can be done. All kinds of new building techniques exist which are more economical and there are new concepts of holding land such as the idea of leasing it, which we do not accept. There are a multitude of new ideas that we could adopt in Canada if we were not operating, as the N.H.A. does, with a set of blinkers over our eyes. This is one area where we must start again under entirely new terms of reference.
In Canada we have never developed a sensible way of financing houses. It has been dealt with in the last 25 years by means of the method of pump priming. When unemployment becomes high we flood the market with mortgage money. This merely results in inflated land and house prices. We have never developed an orderly system for arranging for the financing of homes, and this must be the responsibility of the federal government because nobody else has the capacity. We need a national housing fund, if you want to call it that, which is financed by the government, and the government must be responsible for providing an orderly system of supplying money to builders and individuals for building and buying homes.
Next we must be concerned with the whole method of providing rental homes in Canada. Under the circumstances existing today it may well be that the great North American dream of every man having his castle has disappeared because the costs are becoming so great that most people will probably never be able during their lives to undertake the purchase of a home. As our cities become
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Reid Scott larger and our population grows we are simply going to have to think in terms of different ways of housing people in multiple dwellings or apartments, much as I dislike that idea.
Our national policy in respect of public housing is a disgrace. In the whole of Canada we are not doing the same amount of work or accomplishing as much as some of the cities in the United States. In the whole area of public housing our policy has been a total flop and a national fiasco. The responsibility in this regard rests upon the government here in Ottawa, because it is only here that there is the financial power to promote these types of schemes.
We are doing virtually nothing about the problems of urban development and urban renewal. No matter where you go in the cities in Canada you find they are rotting at the core because of the dilapidation and decay of houses as they get older. I know of no real urban development scheme anywhere in this country that is genuinely being put into effect. Again we must have some leadership in this area.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The seventh point is that we have to start simplifying the regulations. Under the National Housing Act we have tried to process applications. In some cases one must go through 52 different steps in order to process a building program. This takes years and before it is done everybody gives up in disgust and drops the project. This again has to be completely re-examined.
The next matter I wish to mention is the fact that we have done nothing really solid in the way of public housing in Canada. It is given a bad name. Our municipalities will not encourage it because they have an antiquated idea that public housing means a lot of undesirable people and therefore they have a built-in bias against it. We have not been successful either in Ottawa or in the provinces in overcoming this idea.
The eighth point on which I would like to say a few words is the necessity of dealing with the problem of the government's participation in land assembly and land development. Leaving it to private people simply has not worked in this country. This is not a criticism of them. They are in the business to make money. But the net result has been that land assembly and development have been undertaken by private individuals who have been constantly bidding the price up and up and charging what the market will bear.
(Mr. Scott (Danforth).]
Housing lots in metropolitan Toronto which were selling for $4,000 a few years ago are now selling at $12,000 because of the speculation that has gone on. The price of houses will never go down to where ordinary people can buy them unless the government is prepared to take over the land and assemble it.
My next point is that we have to do something about the tremendous responsiblity of the municipalities. Many municipal councils are driven out of their minds by the taxation problems facing them. We have loaded them with all kinds of responsibilities without give-ing them a tax basis upon which to carry them out. For example, it is an anomaly on the North American continent that the cost of education should be borne by the people who are least able to bear it. Almost nowhere else in the world is this the case. We have to re-examine these matters in conjunction with the provinces.
I wish I had more time to discuss some of these problems and I will try to do so on supply motions. These are some of the immediate steps which we could be taking if we were prepared to do so. However, the main problem is that this government will not accept responsibility. It does not take the view that housing is a matter of national importance and national concern. It is, without exception, the greatest social problem facing this country and affecting every Canadian today. Yet the minister in charge of housing goes around the country telling everybody it is a provincial and municipal responsibility. This is a complete negation of the duty which we owe to the people of this country. Before we can hope to accomplish any of these things, and none of them is easy, the government must stand up and be prepared to say that it accepts full responsibility nationally in the field of housing.

A plea for consistency is a novelty from that side of the house. The other day we were told that a cabinet minister can take off his ministerial hat, put on his private hat and make any kind of statement he wishes without having any effect on the government. So consistency is not something about which hon. members on that side should be talking.
May 18. 1967

The Address-Mr. Reid Scott
I see I am almost running out ot time and I want to conclude on a friendly and constructive note, as we always do. We have suggested a full-time minister of housing, which I know many hon. members opposite support and have spoken in favour of in caucus. It is not a novel idea. We know there is good support for it. We hope we will be able to convince the government. They will never solve the housing problems otherwise. We need a minister who can spend all his time roaming around the country trying to co-ordinate all the great jurisdictional problems which we know exist.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Three years ago we asked for a royal commission because we really do not know the problems connected with urbanizing Canada. We need to know what types of housing we are going to require for the next 20 years. We need a blueprint for the next 20 years. We have not done that and we have not got the information. If the government desires, perhaps a special committee of the house, with an adequate staff and facilities to travel, could try to assess the type of program which would be satisfactory to the provinces and in which the provinces would feel we could help without infringing on their jealously guarded jurisdictions.
Everyone agrees that there is a crisis for which no one group can offer a solution. As I said earlier, it is going to require a great partnership, a great deal of co-operation, a great deal of giving on the part of these various jurisdictions. I suggest that even if we started with the best will in the world it would take 10 or 15 years to come to grips adequately with the housing problem. We cannot evade it any longer. We cannot just sit on the sidelines-

speechtext: I should like to thank my colleagues on both sides and I will not take very much more time. What I was trying to say, Mr. Speaker, was that this problem is so critical, so deep rooted, that we cannot sit here in Ottawa and say it is not our problem. Our provinces are desperate for help in this area. Our municipalities are desperate for help in this area, and our people are desperate. I am ashamed, as a Canadian, to go to see how our old age pensioners live. I am saddened to see how our low income people live. I am ashamed of the rotting, decaying centres of our cities. The federal government must assume some responsibility and some leadership. If it does not, the crisis will merely grow and grow. It will never be solved. It will be our shame that one of the most affluent and supposedly advanced nations in the western world did not have the ability or the ingenuity to ascertain how to house its citizens adequately. As I said ealier, if we do not solve this problem, then future parliaments and future Canadians will curse us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join all those who spoke before me in congratulating the mover (Mr. Jamieson) and the seconder (Mr. Cote) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They discharged their duty with eloquence and great distinction.
Mr. Speaker, surely the centennial year will be an excellent occasion, for all Canadians, to strike the balance of achievements and failures having marked the last one hundred years of their history, to look at themselves, to look straight at the country and to consider the means of preparing a future capable of meeting their high aspirations. On this occasion, the question is to examine our past and scrutinize the future, as this will enable us to better understand what we are today and what we must do to become worthy of tomorrow.
Perhaps Canada has not accomplished everything it could have, but if we measure our progress, there is no reason to be pessimistic. There is no need to be ashamed of our past, on the contrary. If we look at what has been done by the 20 million people who succeeded to the 3,635,000 inhabitants of our country a hundred years ago, we see thousands of industries, skyscrapers, railroads, harbours, power plants, asphalt roads used by a great number of car drivers, airfields, thousands of homes and a lot of other things which are that many signs of material progress.
May 18, 1967	COMMONS
We can also see the sun shining on the roofs and spires of thousands of cathedrals, churches, colleges, universities, cultural institutions of all kinds which are a tangible proof of our respect for moral values.
The collective letter published by the Catholic bishops in Canada on the occasion of the centennial of the confederation-a very realistic letter which I should like everyone to read-takes an objective and impartial look at our problems today. The words justice, fraternity and understanding are used again and again in the document.
I shall now quote a passage from the letter:
Canadians today are faced with many problems: incipient inflation, persistent pockets of poverty, economic or political instability. For some, however, the greatest and most difficult problem is to find a solution to the troubles arising in Canada from the coexistence of the two main linguistic and cultural groups which, strangely enough, constitute two opposing majority groups.
In some ways, this is a very basic human problem, for it involves important values and concerns people both materially and spiritually.
The bishops consider that the disquiet now prevalent in the Canadian community arises, on the one hand, from the dissatisfaction of an increasing number of French Canadians with the problems facing their ethnic group in their search for fulfilment and, on the other hand, from the concern entertained in other areas of Canada over their demands.
Consideration is also given the problems of minorities and I quote:
The minorities living in Canada are not all in the same position. Care must be taken to guarantee fair treatment to each of them and the sacrifices such treatment involves in the cost of some services, education for instance, in the provinces, must be accepted.
The prelates give us a warning and I quote:
Canadians will live through dark days, through fruitless and impoverishing strife, unless the various groups inhabiting their country, particularly the two main linguistic and cultural groups, cannot accept and recognize without reserve or misunderstanding the legitimacy of their differences and of their own destiny and if they fail to accept, in mutual respect of their rights, the compromises required by their special position.
Mr. Speaker, residents of Canada may have different traditions, cultures, religions, forbears and incomes, but they must feel they are essential parts of the Canadian community.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
There is talk of separatism, of an associate state, but our whole history proves that breaking up Canada in small states would be like snuffing the candles in a castle, blowing
DEBATES	363
The Address-Mr. Matte them out one by one until the whole castle is in the dark.
I say and repeat that if as much had been done previously as the Pearson government has since achieved toward a better understanding of the French-Canadian people, of the aspirations of the French Canadians and of the province of Quebec, there would be no question today of separatism, associate state nor, for some people, of joining the United States.
The province of Quebec has no desire for a special status, although it is not a province like the others. It does not look for privileges but it wants its right to be respected 100 per cent; just as it respects the rights of others, it wants the rights of the French Canadians respected throughout Canada.
Doubtless, the constitution needs some changes, some explaining. Indeed, each new act adds something to it and even now we are having a closer look at the fundamental problem.
Mr. Speaker, to love one's country is, among other things, to know what it was, to know what it is and whit it can become, and then to reach for the indicated ideal. With some perspicacity, and the firm and generous resolution to do the utmost, Canada can achieve great things in its second century, achievements which Canadians can be proud of when the second century is celebrated.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my remarks, I would like to say a few words about my constituency of Champlain. All our rural parishes, all our small communities want industries that will enable them to develop. They are ready to any sacrifices necessary, and they await with anxiety the industrialists and industries that our governments could send to them. We have a sound population, and it is unfortunate that the people in each parish cannot develop for themselves a future at home.
Many of them, mostly sons of farmers, have to migrate to larger centres, often increasing the number of unemployed.
I asked the Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury) to declare the whole new Champlain county a designated area. Part of it is already designated; the rest should also be designated, and this is urgent. I refer specifically to that part of the county of Portneuf that will fall in the county of Champlain. Several industries, one of which is one hundred years old, were shut down, leaving the population unemployed and in a disquieting economic situation.
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Orange
In the past, I also talked about expanding the port of Trois-Rivieres to the east, that is at Ste. Marthe, of Cap de la Madeleine, as a means of developing the northern economy. We are still waiting, and I think that the matter has been under consideration for quite a long time.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to repeat the speech I made the last day of the last session about agriculture. An amendment was moved by the opposition, but it was strictly for political and partisan purposes; that is why I voted against it, because this government has done more for agriculture in eastern Canada than any other government.
Our friends opposite are ready to do anything today and they criticize-which is an easy thing to do. However, what did they do for our eastern farmers when they were in power and even had an absolute power?
I recognize that the new dairy policy, although not complete, is a step forward, but it does not meet fully the requests which were made. The matter of quotas, especially, is a puzzle-for instance, the withdrawal of the subsidy on surplus liquid milk. But I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is doing and will continue to do everything in his power to give as much satisfaction as possible.
On May 24 next, that is next week, the farmers will march on parliament. We shall be very happy and very proud to receive them.
