speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join other members of the house in congratulating the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson), and also the seconder, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote) on the fine contribution they made to this debate. As one who is relatively new to this house, and having heard only one other debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I must say that I think the standard set by the mover and seconder will be held in high regard in the years to come.
In the course of this debate many members have made most appropriate references to the role of parliament as it exists in the twentieth century and as we move toward the twenty first century. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) set out a 15-point program dealing with what he thought

would speed up and possibly modernize the effectiveness of parliament. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in his thoughtful presentation last week outlined his views on committee responsibility and on the role of the private member of parliament and his relationship to the executive.
We have also discussed the use of television both in the house and in committees. Yesterday, I believe, one hon. member suggested that the government might examine the kind of facilities that are available to members of parliament in Canada compared with those available to their counterparts in the United States.
As one who is attending his first parliament I must say that I was somewhat surprised and possibly a little disappointed with the kind of assistance and benefits-I am not talking of financial benefits-afforded to hon. members. Having been elected for the first time a member approaches his new role with a great deal of enthusiasm and, hopefully, energy. Suddenly he finds himself in the position at times of feeling frustrated by his inability not only to do the kind of job he hoped to do but just to carry out those responsibilities which the people who voted for him in his constituency asked him to undertake. There has been a great deal of discussion along this line. My only contribution at this stage is to say that I hope the discussion will continue and that as a result the facilities available, particularly to private members of parliament, the backbenchers, will improve in years to come so that we may do what we were sent here to do by the people who sent us.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I was greatly relieved, Mr. Speaker, as was the mineral industry of Canada, by the announcement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) made earlier in the session. The concern caused by certain recommendations of the Carter commission on taxation with respect to the mineral industry was such that some believed that this year's exploration program in some parts of the country would be seriously curtailed. I refer to the possibility of changes in the tax structure affecting that industry. The minister's announcement, made without prejudicing the government's final decision, helped to resolve some of the concern felt by the industry. In considering the recommendations to which I have alluded, particularly those dealing with the tax free period, I hope that the government and its advisers will consider carefully any changes
May 18, 1967

to be made and will make only those changes that benefit the development of this major industry in our country.
Let us look for a moment at what the mineral industry means to Canada. In 1966 the value of mineral production, which amounted to 7.2 per cent of the gross national product, was approximately $4 billion, eight times the 1945 dollar value. This does not include moneys expended on exploration and development, nor goods and services associated with the industry. The industry has been of basic importance in the economic development of Canada, being the second leading industry in terms of dollar earnings. At the same time it is not without serious problems. It has a labour shortage partly because of the nature of the industry and also because of where some mining developments are located. The spectre of the Carter commission hangs over its head. Finally, certain sections of the industry such as gold mining are plagued with special problems of prices and costs. I hope the cost-aid program for the gold mining industry will be continued and possibly expanded. Otherwise a number of communities throughout Canada will be affected seriously.
I heard with a great deal of interest the announcement of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) in the house regarding the off-reserve Indian housing program which, as has been openly acknowledged, is long overdue. It will assist the Indian residents of Canada to move to areas of economic opportunity away from the traditional reserves. Most important, I believe the program will aid young Indians who wish on completion of their education to work in metropolitan or other areas of Canada and find opportunities to make a decent start in life in the same way as many of us have been helped by our parents to get off the ground.
I asked the minister if a similar program could not apply to the Eskimos. In asking that question I was concerned about the Eskimo people who leave their homes and hunting communities to move to areas of economic opportunity. I think particularly of the Eskimo people working on the Great Slave Lake railway which is operated almost entirely by Eskimo employees. I think also of the Eskimo working in the mines at Yellowknife and Lynn Lake, Manitoba. All these people want to integrate into the community in which they live. Quite apart from the problems of language and culture are the problems of becoming established in a community,
The Address-Mr. Orange and I think that the government and all Canadians have a responsibility to help in the initial process of integration.
In 1963 a number of Eskimo families were moved to Yellowknife to work in the mines. In the four intervening years some have returned to their original homes at Rankin Inlet and Keewatin and others have persevered. Those who have are first class miners who earn bonuses larger than those earned by the majority of their fellow employees. Yet because they have large families they are expected to live in accommodation which, to my way of thinking, is inadequate. What does one say to a man who approaches and says, "I want to stay here in Yellowknife so that my children can go to school, so that they can have the same chance your children have, but I must have a decent place to live in"? If the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development were in the house I would appeal to him to extend his program to people such as I have just described. I also asked the minister if he had any plans regarding the Metis people and I did so recognizing that the government of Canada does not have responsibility for these people. Their education, welfare and economic development are the responsibility of the province in which they live and they are treated as other citizens of that province are treated. I regret that the Metis, who did so much to open up the west and north in early days, have become the forgotten people of our nation and I hope that in our centennial year the government of Canada, in co-operation with the provinces, will put aside political differences, will not ask who will pay for what, but will try to work out a viable, exciting and dynamic solution to help the Metis of Canada to enter the mainstream of the life of our nation in the same way as it will help the Indians and, I hope, the Eskimos in the years to come.
In the first session of this parliament we enacted legislation amending the Northwest Territories Act. Though, as was said, it was housekeeping legislation, it did something that was most important. It extended the franchise, the right to vote, throughout the Northwest Territories. Up to that time people who were living in Keewatin and the eastern Arctic could not vote in territorial elections although they could in federal elections. Since then there have been exciting developments. The franchise has indeed been extended and an election held. Three representatives from the Arctic region sat with the council at the last two sessions, one held at Resolute Bay
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Orange and the other in Ottawa. Yellowknife was declared the capital of the Northwest Territories and the governor of the territories was moved from the south, from beneath the umbrella of the federal administration, to the north. At the same time an announcement was made that as a result of the recommendations of the Carrothers commission on government in the Northwest Territories a white paper would be produced setting out, in effect, the government's position with respect to the over-all development of government in the north.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I appeal to the cabinet to ensure that this white paper becomes a centennial project and thus a centennial present to the people of the north to assist them in getting their territorial government on the ground. I hope this white paper will be available not later than the coming fall. I also hope that when the white paper is available and open for discussion the views of northerners are taken into account. I expect they will be. Knowing the manner in which government sometimes tends to operate, however, I think it should be clear that if the views expressed in the white paper do not reflect the views of northerners there might be problems about approving the kind of legislation brought forward to bring government to the north.
In the course of the decision to declare Yellowknife the capital, the town of Fort Smith became concerned, not because it was not to be the capital but with respect to its future. Positive steps have been taken by the territorial government to ensure that this community will continue to grow as a northern settlement. I should like to think that the federal government, recognizing its responsibility because it made the decision, will continue to provide the impetus necessary to assist the town planners in that community to solve the problems they now face. I trust the federal government will make a decision regarding the future of Fort Smith.
I am happy to see the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) in the house because I wish to pay him a compliment which I hope will result in the continuation of the good work which has been done by the department in the last few months in the north. I refer to the decrease in parcel post rates and air freight rates which has taken place as a result of an evaluation of postal facilities and charges by the department. However, I suggest that the steps the minister has taken are not sufficient. We still suffer from an irregular service and a lack of

proper post office facilities in many places. There are even inconsistencies in the new rate structure which has been established. The Postmaster General assured me that he is undertaking a further study of postal services in northern Canada the results of which will be available in the fall.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation began television service in Yellowknife on May 14. We now have one station in the north and the corporation is to be commended for its forward approach. We know there is another station planned for the Lynn Lake area and a third for the Seven Islands area. We hope the C.B.C.'s plans to provide television service for the larger communities in the isolated northern areas of our nation by means of a "frontier package" will move ahead quickly. When I realized the cost of setting up one of these small package units and maintaining it for a year I became concerned lest the corporation might not move ahead as quickly as we would like it to do.
In the course of the past month the Department of Manpower and Immigration has opened employment offices in the Northwest Territories. This development will go a long way toward resolving some of the problems connected with local hire with which we in the north are faced. All too often in the past, particularly in connection with construction programs, contractors from the south have brought complete labour forces into the area thus denying the opportunity of employment to our own people. Among the greatest offenders have been oil exploration companies-at great cost to themselves, I may add.
I should like for a moment to examine the government's external aid program in relation to the development program designed to help underdeveloped areas in this country. We know that this year the external aid program will contribute through grants, loans and direct aid approximately $300 million to the development of nations throughout the world. I think this is the least Canada can do. We like to think of ourselves as an affluent nation and if we wish to take our place in the community of nations we must also accept some responsibility. The only complaint with regard to aid being granted outside our borders is that perhaps it is too little.
There is, however, one aspect which bothers me, and I know it bothers many who live in the northern territories. With so many things needing to be done in terms of northern development in order to allow those who
May 18. 1967	COMMONS
live there, particularly the Eskimos, the Indians and the Metis, to enjoy a reasonable standard of living, the northern development budget could surely be increased by more than 5 per cent a year, the total amount of the increase which took place last year, bearing in mind that the external aid budget has increased by some $50 million a year. Yet in the last four years the budget has doubled from about $16 million a year to $32 million in terms of real federal expenditures, not including provincial expenditures.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The throne speech made reference to a system of industrial incentives to encourage development of regional economic growth and to encourage further development in the north, and it was suggested that by regional economic planning some of these incentives might come into being. What I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, is whether this is to be merely an extension of the many federal programs such as aid to industry, rural development and designated areas, which do not apply north of the sixtieth parallel, or is this something new and exciting that the government is proposing? I sincerely hope it is a combination of both.
There is a tendency on the part of many people to suggest that because the population of the north is small, which we acknowledge, what we as a nation are doing for the north is adequate. Maybe this would be true if we were talking in terms of numbers of people, but I suggest that what we are seeking is not only growth in our population but greater investment in the growth and development of Canada as a whole. We hope that when the time comes that the vast mineral resources of the north are being fully exploited-we see One example in the Pine Point development where as a result of the opening up of this one mine the mineral production of the north tripled in the space of one short year-the north in turn will be able to repay not only the contribution made by the nation to its development but also assist in the growth of the country as a whole. It is on this basis that I draw the comparison between what we are doing in external aid and what I would like to see happen in the northern territories. The programs of government have been good but we have a long way to go.
Housing for our Indian people does not compare with the liberal program that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development introduced for the Eskimo people and yet, Mr. Speaker, I ask what is the
DEBATES	367
The Address-Mr. Orange advantage of building a home if water, supplies, garbage disposal and electricity are not available or are available only in a pretty primitive way? In the settlement of Inuvik, now the town of Inuvik, a number of local people, Indian, Eskimo, Metis and white, banded together in 1963 to launch a co-operative housing program. Inuvik is a town which was built by the government in the last decade to take account of the need of the government for an administrative centre in the Mackenzie delta. The town was built in two ways. Members of the northern affairs committee who visited it saw how this was done. I refer to the serviced area and the unserviced area. By this I mean that government employees live in modern standard housing serviced by water and sewers through a very practical although expensive utilidor system, which also includes heating arrangements, but the people who come from the Mackenzie delta by and large live in the west end where there are no services other than a primitive trucked water supply and a pretty basic garbage disposal system.
The members of this co-operative, all of whom are fully employed, have been pressing the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for three years in order that at their own expense they too might enjoy the very basic amenity of being able to turn on a tap in their kitchens and have running water. But this year again, and for reasons which I do not know except possibly the old chestnut that it might cost too much, the government has indicated to the local residents, according to an editorial in the Inuvik newspaper, the Drum, that possibly next year but not this year something will be made available to the people who live in the co-operative development.
These people want facilities, Mr. Speaker. They are prepared to pay for them. All I suggest is that somehow or other, in co-operation with the federal government in particular and with the territorial government where necessary, some system be worked out to provide basic services to the people who were born and brought up in the north, who are making their whole living in the north and who feel they should have the same opportunities as their white cousins or their cousins who come from the south and who live in modern fully serviced government housing while working for the government.
We can also look across the Arctic to a community called Eskimo Point in Keewatin. A new housing program is intended for that

May 18, 1967
The Address-Mr. Noble community this year, but when we ask about water, garbage and sewage services we get the answer that they really are not available. From Eskimo Point it is eight miles to the nearest lake where water is available. In wintertime ice is cut from a lake closer to the settlement. This might not be of much concern except for the fact that over the years this community has suffered a series of medical disasters to the point that in 1963 half of the population was moved to a hospital in the south because of an outbreak of meningitis and tuberculosis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join all other members of the House of Commons who have offered congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I admire their worthy contributions.
The speech from the throne was only an exercise in words and it was very disappointing. People across this nation had expectations of a masterpiece on this special occasion that would overshadow any previous effort. During this centennial year, when Canada is receiving unprecedented world recognition, there is a rare opportunity for the government to spread its wings and introduce a program that would stir the heart and soul of every Canadian. Mr. Speaker, the government is negative in regard to that imagination which would visualize Canada's vast potential for her second century. The government's brain trust, with several years at their disposal to prepare another manifesto of action, have come up with another failure.
This is also a time for reflection, and at the beginning of our second century of confederation it is fitting that we pay tribute to those Canadians who have gone before, even to those who laid the foundations of this nation many years before confederation. Many of our forebears came to Canada to escape oppression and injustice, to a land where a new life could be lived in freedom. This was a way of life in which they took great pride and they sought to preserve it at any cost. The fathers of confederation, in their deliberations and when setting up their statutes, made freedom the first principle.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We have fought in two terrible wars involving the supreme sacrifice of thousands of our people in defence of freedom. Canadians are well aware of the price of this God-given right. Surely we cannot continue to stand by and watch it disappear piecemeal by regimentation and legislation. The philosophy of the
[Mr. Orange.)
government is progressively removing the challenge from our way of life. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how far can we continue on the course charted by this government and have any real freedom left?
I bring to the government's attention those wise and enduring words of Abraham Lincoln when he said:
You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift: you cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong: you cannot help the wage-earner by pulling down the wagepayer: you cannot further the brotherhood of man by encouraging class hatred. You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich: you cannot keep out of trouble by spending more than you earn. You cannot build character and courage by taking away man's initiative and independence. You cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves.
There is at least one cabinet minister who has registered some anxiety about the course of events in this nation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), when speaking to a Toronto Rotary Club a few days ago, said:
I am a businessman at heart and I believe it is the responsibility of the government to bring revenues and expenditures into balance and provide a balanced budget.
He stated further that the government must encourage exports and in so doing could build a good surplus on its trading account which would help reduce our international account deficit. He contends that most governments spend more than they should. Canadians, he said, are enjoying the second or third highest standard of living in the world, although we are living on borrowed money. The minister insisted that Canada must maintain a climate that is favourable to foreign investment. If we do not, he said, we just do not balance our international books. However, with foreign investment Canada gets a large measure of foreign ownership, which raises questions as to whether she is in danger of losing economic and political sovereignty. The trade minister said his own view is that it is not the fact of foreign ownership that matters but what use is made of the ownership. He also said that more than 99 per cent of the foreign-owned firms in Canada are good corporate citizens from a Canadian point of view. This minister, Mr. Speaker, is a sound businessman and the treasury benches are in short supply of men of his calibre. It must also be evident to the minister that the spiralling tax burden must be brought under control. Our tax bill, compared with that of other democratic countries
May 18, 1967	COMMONS
such as the United States, Japan and Australia, is already away out of line.
Another cabinet minister, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon), speaking in London last Friday said that there would be further government intervention in the economy and that a reasonably courageous government will not listen to complaints about high taxes from businessmen and the public at large. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) on one or more occasions has stated that a man should be guaranteed a livelihood whether or not he wants to work. No wonder we have many people who do not want to work. Such statements indicate that there is an urgent need for good businessmen on the front benches opposite. This government operates the biggest business in the nation; yet from all appearances it has phased out good business principles.
We have now arrived at the position where it takes one third of our gross national product to pay our taxes, and the trend can only continue upward. This fact was borne out on a recent television program when a commentator interviewed the Registrar General (Mr. Turner), a prominent, young minister of the crown. The give-away program he said he would support will make the socialists look like pikers.
This cradle to the grave security will certainly kill initiative and along with all the other lavish spending will eventually bring this nation to the point of no return. There is a faction in the government leaning far to the left. Their statements and actions leave no doubt as to their philosophy. Others are extreme socialists at heart but do not have the intestinal fortitude to be vocal at this time. However, their performance before being elevated to posts of influence leaves no doubt about their philosophy.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada last March expressed his concern over the fact that Canadian costs and prices rose faster last year than productivity and that demands placed on the economy outstripped the economy's ability to produce. Ironically enough, the governor's warning of economic stress and strain coincided with the government's disclosure of its spending program for 1967-68. This was an unprecedented government housekeeping bill for $11J billion with a good possibility of $250 million to $300 million more to be tacked on before this year is over.
In 1963 the Glassco report called for major cuts in our large and often inefficient civil
DEBATES	369
The Address-Mr. Noble service. It has become a top-heavy bureaucracy. Instead the government has increased the civil service by 71,445 since October 1, 1964. New departments appear to be the order of the day and indications are that thousands more will join the civil service within the next few months. Mr. Glassco claimed that savings of $500 million could be effected annually if his recommendations to streamline government were implemented. The government has been slow to take action on these recommendations, and 150 of them have not been implemented.
There is a proverb that sums up in a few words this government's position.
We do not what we ought,
What we ought not we do.
And lean upon the thought That chance will bring us through.
I am privileged to be a member of the public accounts committee and am deeply concerned and astonished, as the people across this nation must be, at the many items of careless and extravagant spending by the government. The Auditor General has made these revelations to the committee, which in turn submitted strong corrective recommendations. But the reaction of the government has been indifference. Repercussions to the government's actions are beginning to register right across the country. One day last week Premier Bennett of British Columbia said that federal waste, extravagance and patronage are costing the taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
This government talks about a better way of life for Canadians. What is being done about it? Every part of the nation is in need of housing. This problem has reached emergency proportions; therefore every obstacle should be removed. Removal of the sales tax from housebuilding materials should take effect at once. Builders should be mobilized in areas where the need is most urgent.
We are worried about our talented young people migrating to the United States. This can be expected, and even more so if they cannot secure the first requirement here at home, namely, a roof over their heads. This raises the matter of immigration. How can we justify enticing more people to our land when housing accommodation is not available? If the government had really taken the welfare of the people of this nation to heart, this centennial year would have been the milestone in our history when all our people were provided with respectable housing. We have
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Noble all the elements in human and material resources but the leadership is conspicuous by its absence.
I turn now to another serious problem that involves every citizen of this nation. I refer to safety on our highways. I believe I made the initial approach to the government on this matter by way of a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in 1963. I have continued to request action on the various aspects of the problem by way of questions in every session since that time. On February 2, 1966, I brought to the attention of the house viewpoints on highway safety as expressed by the provincial minister of highways, Chief Justice McRuer, the commissioner of the R.C.M.P., and the chief coroner of metro Toronto.
It has been proven that drunk drivers and air pollution from carbonmonoxide are creating the greatest hazards. My questioning has been concentrated on these two problems because statistics have shown that only one per cent of highway accidents can be attributed to defective automobiles. Other members of the house have joined in the crusade to reduce the tragic death toll on our highways, but the government has declined to take action on one particular matter that would have a telling effect. I refer to making the breath-alizer test mandatory. I urged the government to take this action many months ago, and no reason has been given for the delay.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Surely the government does not fear the liquor and beer interests, or are they hesitating hoping that the provinces will take this responsibility? Such legislation has proven useful and successful in New York and other states, so I see no valid reason why it should not be given favourable consideration here.
Over 5,000 people were killed on our highways last year and in over 50 per cent of these fatalities alcohol was involved. There were also 160,000 or more injured, many permanently. Liquor would also account for more than half of these. The law will not tolerate such behaviour on trains, planes or in industry. It is beyond me why the government treats the matter so lightly. Rather, the government is showing great concern for the welfare of criminals when it proposes to bring up the matter of the abolition of capital punishment again. It has ignored the decision already made and wants to have the matter decided again.

I am concerned about the problems of the farmers and the need for a constant supply of food to take care of our domestic needs with enough to continue to fulfil our obligations to our customers and other needy people. There is a tremendous migration from rural to urban life, partly due to uneconomic units but chiefly on account of better rewards for an hour of work. Governments cannot continue to ignore the just requests of agriculturalists without jeopardizing our food production.
Next week we will witness a march on parliament hill in protest against a poorly conceived dairy policy. It seems the minister was ill advised and the proposition he put forward brought scorn upon his head. On this occasion the minister might have been in a more favourable position if he had paid attention to the practical information made available to him. I believe it to be the urgent responsibility of the government, especially of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), to be on hand to meet the farmers on May 24, a date they have designated well in advance and one that comes at a time when there is a lapse in their seeding activities. I make a strong appeal for favourable consideration of the request that will be made regarding the price of milk. If the farmers were paid on the same basis as industrial workers, even without giving any consideration for their large investment the price of milk would be higher than what they are proposing. These people are essential to the health and welfare of this nation.
This government is so neglectful on many occasions that a crisis develops before any attention is given to the problem. The militia had to be called out in Ireland a few days ago to restore order when the farmers' requests there were ignored. We would not like this to happen in Canada, especially in our centennial year.
Milk producers plan their operations for months in advance and it was folly for the Minister of Agriculture to expect our farmers to accept a drastic change in policy without a protest. The sudden announcement that quotas for manufacturing milk produced in 1967 and 1968 will be based on 1966-67 production means a substantial drop in their incomes and it was especially disappointing to those who had increased their herds. The fluid milk producers felt that a reasonable period of adjustment should have been provided in respect of terminating the federal subsidy. The government is now faced with a disagreeable incident created by their own procrastination and poor judgment.
May 18, 1967	COMMONS
In conclusion I want to say that I am proud to be a Canadian, as I am sure we all are, and I believe we would all agree we have the best country in the world. We have the potential for a future of fullness and plenty. We are richly endowed with vast renewable natural resources in our agriculture, our fisheries, our forests and our waters. It is our responsiblity to see that these riches are preserved and improved for posterity. We must also rally round those leaders who will preserve the freedom of the individual so that he may be privileged to develop his own life, his own talents and his own self-expression with special privileges to no one.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Maiheson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I pay heartfelt tributes to both the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I doubt that anyone reading Hansard will fully sense the command of this house obtained by both those able speakers, speaking as I recall without notes but with enthusiasm in developing their thoughts. It is my belief that the mover, with carefully chosen words, expressed what was very much in the hearts of us all.
In referring to the speech delivered by His Excellency on Monday, May 8, I find these words:
A country is a home; it must be built and furnished for the good life of its people.
His Excellency concluded his memorable address with words of the first Governor General of our country uttered some 100 years ago. He said:
-a blessing to yourselves and your posterity, and a fresh starting point in the moral, political and material advancement of the people of Canada.
The subject I should like to deal with briefly is penitentiaries and parole. As we start out on a new century I think we would do well to face seriously the problems relating to crime and punishment in Canada. I rejoice in the fact that on January 1, 1966, the government saw fit to make a full department of the office of the Solicitor General and that as a result penitentiaries and parole now fall under the jurisdiction of the new minister and deputy minister. I am also pleased that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who have been such an important element as anti-crime experts in maintaining the good life in Canada over the past 100 years and more, now balance the punishment side of the department engaged in incarcerating the offender and assisting him later by way of parole.
DEBATES	371
The Address-Mr. Matheson
The minister who is responsible in this regard I know is determined to play an extremely important role. I have read several speeches delivered by the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), some of which have been published, and I find him to be a thoughtful, philosophical and idealistic man who is quietly and very successfully accomplishing reform in this long neglected field.
It is a fact that no one likes to oversee prisons. We all seek to avoid looking at the unpleasant. I happen to know that very few members of this parliament or the parliament which preceded it in the last few years have visited federal penitentiaries. There are some who have made a study of our institutions but by and large even members of parliament, who are their brothers' keepers in this regard, have taken little time out to visit the penitentiaries, save happily for the penitentiary committee. What can be said about members of parliament applies with even more force to society generally.
The Solicitor General is reported in the Optimist magazine of June, 1966, as having asked this important question: "What does Canada owe her criminals?" Then he reviews briefly something of the history of punishment in this country. He told us that in the ancient world the generally accepted idea was that a prison was regarded solely as a useful means of safe custody pending trial or punishment. It was not thought to suffice as a form of punishment in itself because in early days death was the penalty provided for most offences. There are records throughout Canada of the harsh penalties that were then imposed.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
He writes that when England began at last to move away from the death penalty it moved toward the more humane concepts of banishment and transportation. Finally, imprisonment was accepted as punishment. Incarceration in prison changed, at last, quite naturally toward the present day advocacy that the prison should not function merely as a place of confinement for docile, well disciplined human beings but instead should be a dynamic place, a laboratory in which character disorders and anti-social attitudes are examined under the microscope of modern knowledge, a workshop in which twisted personalities are straightened and disoriented men and women are given some sense of direction.
May 18. 1967

The Address-Mr. Matheson
I was intrigued by the article written by J. Alex Edmison, Q.C., of the national parole board on crime and its treatment in Canada. He writes about the various alternatives to imprisonment which have been fully tested in Canada. These penalties applied in Ontario, Quebec and other parts of our country long before confederation. There was the pillory in which a man was held firmly by the neck and wrists. People could assist in the punishment either by whip or by throwing something at the man. The pillory was abolished in Canada by statute in 1842. The stocks were used in upper Canada in 1804. William Lyon Mackenzie, carrying out his duties as first mayor of Toronto, presided over magistrate's court in 1834 and required a man to suffer this ignominious treatment. It was abandoned in England in 1872. Branding was a very common punishment. In 1798 the Chief Justice of Upper Canada had criminals branded in open court. The practice was abolished in 1802, except for manslaughter. Banishment, of course, was a common punishment, and so was transportation.
1 mention these specific punishments because when we look back over the short period of a century it is clear that the penitentiary has been a rather late sociological device to punish and reform the prisoner. I think that by now we have had sufficient time to make certain deliberate estimates of the efficacy of this form of punishment. Inherent in everything I say must be the question: Why do we punish at all? What is the philosophic or moral reason for the punishment of a person who has breached a code which we call the Criminal Code? I suppose of the traditional explanations, one is based on retribution or revenge, another on deterrence and still another on the rehabilitation factor and together the protection of society at large.
But it would be well for us, as modern people with modern problems and a new sense of total responsibility for the ills of our society, to consider the total cost of the program, the penitentiary approach to punishment. It might surprise Canadians to know that the cost of a cell in a maximum security institution is now between $20,000 and $25,000. The cost per year for an inmate in a maximum security institution today is approximately $3,650, or $10 a day, which is not really an unusual price for a hotel room. In the case of an inmate with a wife and dependent children the total cost to Canada, to the province and to the municipality can often reach the annual figure of $10,000. The desira-
ble size of a penitentiary does not exceed 450 inmates and any institution of that size now costs approximately $10 million. But by way of dramatic contrast I would invite Canadians to note the fact that the cost of a paroled prisoner is approximately $250 per year. Perhaps it is my highland background, but something in all these figures worries me a great deal. Imprisonment is costly.
A few days ago I spoke to the John Howard Society in Fredericton. My remarks were reported in the Daily Gleaner under the headline "Men Want to be Forgiven". This brought a few letters which I read with some interest. In one letter was an editorial from the Gleaner of April 24,	1967, titled
"Kindness To Criminals", the final paragraph of which reads as follows:
We believe that criminals should bear the stigma for their crimes, and that this is not only a part of their punishment but a part of the protection of the innocent.
I quite understand how it is that an editorial writer who is on the outside and knows something about the statistics of crime in North America, particularly in the United States, or the crime statistics in Great Britain, could come to the conclusion that harshness presents some sort of solution. But the real fact is that our prisons are not succeeding. The recidivist rate, that is, the rate at which persons go to penitentiary after having been in prison before, remains constant at approximately 80 per cent. On the other hand, the parole failure rate in Canada stands constant at the figure of 10 per cent.
I believe that through the efforts of the Solicitor General and the type of program that is at last being implemented we are seeking to close this gap. We hope to drop the parole success rate of 90 per cent and thereby substantially reduce the recidivist rate and thus sharply reduce the cost to the taxpayer. However, my argument is based not on vulgar economics, important as they may be, but on something which I think is very much more important than economy, namely, rehabilitation. After we have examined these figures carefully we must come to the conclusion that locking people up does not solve very much.
I was interested in the report appearing in the Ottawa Citizen today of the address John Braithwaite, our expert on corrections, gave to the annual meeting of the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa last evening. He made the point that the basic danger is that the offender is psychologically cut off from society. He
May 18/ 1967

pointed out that throughout the world there is growing criticism of and inquiry into the traditional methods of reform. Exactly the same kind of inquiry is proceeding presently in the office of the Solicitor General. He speaks about the trend toward increasing community involvement. He mentions certain organizations, societies and groups that must become involved in rehabilitation. I could not agree more, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Throughout Canada and the United States and particularly in northwestern Europe studies and experiments have been conducted on the subject of rehabilitation. You even find this same spirit of reform, the trend toward rehabilitation and the tendency to the people out of institutions just as rapidly as possible, in the far east. I think it was Winston Churchill who said more eloquently than I could, that you assess and judge a society by the manner in which that society cares for those people who are held in custody.
I was delighted by the scholarly and wise address given on civil liberties by my colleague the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald). It seems to me that crime and punishment is closely related to the attitude we entertain toward civil liberties. I believe when we look at the special problems of the offender we would be wise to make comparisons with other exceptional or different people in the community.
I admire, sir, the work that is done in the town of Smiths Falls where there is a hospital carrying the considerable burden of the care of retarded children for the province of Ontario. The magazine, "Canada's Mental Health", had a special issue in November on mental retardation. In it I find an article by an old friend. Dr. H. F. Frank, a psychiatrist who has devoted himself to the care of the retarded. Speaking of the disability of mental retardation, Dr. Frank said:
The idea that a child who cannot come up to average community requirements should be "put away" in an institution, dies very hard... We are just beginning to learn that a large number of exceptional children must be integrated into every day community life and helped to achieve the best of their ability ... Working an ill adapted child into society cannot be achieved only through institutionalization ... the community has to realize that a large number of children should continue to live in the community where their educational, recreational and other needs must be met.
Anyone who goes to Smiths Falls and sees what has been done in that institution for thousands of unfortunate exceptional little
The Address-Mr. Matheson people, some of whom stay there for many years and become exceptional older people, will appreciate that it is not possible for us to send all our troubles to one community and hope that that community, with all the medical skills it may possess, the devotion, the care and concern and loving attention, can right these wrongs. I would urge, with John Braithwaite, that the time has come in Canada when there must be a much larger element of total involvement in problems of problem people-both patients and prisoners. Years ago Eugene Debs said, "While there is a soul in prison I am not free."
The fact is that many of the best people in our Canadian society do not care about this prisoner problem, do not know anything about the problem and never have become involved. We have, therefore, the extraordinary situation of recidivism staying at the high figure of 80 per cent and parole staying at the low rate of 10 per cent. Society tries to protect itself against these evil and different people getting out and being rehabilitated simply because as a society we are not prepared to share the burdens, the risks and the responsibility of making rehabilitation work. We take a false pride in our low rate of parole failure. Someone has suggested the analogy of a baseball player with an exceptionally high batting average being kept out of the game and on the bench to maintain his high batting average.
We are proud of our parole service. We are proud of our penitentiary service. Of course, both of these could be better than they are just as anything we do could be better. I feel we have come to the point where collectively we must take the risk and share in the responsibility of a much higher parole failure rate in the hope that we substantially reduce the recidivist rate. Although it may not be obvious to everybody this is what the Solicitor General has begun to do. During the few months in which he has held this portfolio he has already managed to accomplish a great deal. It may not be known, but he has already caused a larger number of people to be paroled. Although it is difficult to obtain these highly qualified people, he has taken on more parole officers. These are specialized social workers.
The fact is that the increased number of paroles has not resulted in any marked increase in the failure rate. In spite of our sharply increased population and particularly juvenile population, the number of inmates in federal institutions has declined this year by
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Matheson approximately 500. I should like to see an even sharper decline. This has been accomplished by a process of segregation, determining whether a person must be cared for custodially or in some rehabilitation centre.
We must acknowledge there are some people who are not likely to be redeemed. However, I believe many more can be rehabilitated than has been achieved in the past. Last week I spent some hours with the warden of Joyceville. We had a long talk about the successes and failures of that institution. He speaks with a background of 25 years experience and a recollection of the various things that have been done during his service to improve vitally the facilities for effecting reform. He told me how much the penitentiary officers care about their work. Basically the thing that counts is personal involvement. He referred to his wife Stella. He said that Stella had no particular training in penology and had never taken a course in psychology. He mentioned the number of people in the institution whom Stella had befriended, in some cases elderly men committed to a life of crime, a life of failure. She had brought them into her home. She had trusted them and reached out to them. This made all the difference. The victories were personal victories.
There is only one way to redeem people, I believe, and that is by recognizing the person as an individual. One of the letters I received from Fredericton tells me what is really needed is hope. This person writes that the prisoner has lost hope, a lot of people have lost hope and find it hard, if not impossible, to get it back. According to the ancient legend, Mr. Speaker, Pandora was a woman whose curiosity caused her to slip off the cover of the jar containing a multitude of plagues for hapless man, namely, gout, rheumatism, colic, envy, spite and revenge and many other ills. Pandora hastened to replace the lid but all these evils had escaped and were scattered far and wide. Only one thing remained at the bottom of the jar-hope. So to this way, whatever mischief is abroad, while we have hope we are not entirely wretched. Some men in our institutions have lives which have been confounded by illness, hatred, mischief and malice. If we seek to build the good society we must build on individual lives and on the only foundation of character that remains -hope.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Our neighbour to the south has started to show the way. The United States federal department of justice was permitted as of 1965

to release incarcerated offenders to work in the community and return to custody at night. This many sound revolutionary to Canadians, Mr. Speaker, but other countries do likewise. As of now over 2,000 persons have been involved in this United States program. Their gross earnings are in excess of $2,147,000. Of this sum, $203,000 went to pay their room and board at the penitentiary $303,000 was paid by way of various state and federal taxes, and what was left over went to support the inmates' families or to await and to hasten their day of release.
Not many weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, I was in a penitentiary at Taipei which housed over 2,000 men and women. Bear in mind that our institutions house approximately 450 inmates. This institution was built at very low cost in our terms, something like a quarter of a million dollars in American money. It had no armed guards. I was in a concert hall with over 500 prisoners present listening to a 15-piece orchestra with one custodial officer in attendance unarmed. There were many women prisoners. The social conditions of the country were such that these women prisoners, who were mainly narcotic addicts, were compelled to bring their children to the penitentiary to reside with them.
Does this sound shocking, Mr. Speaker? In fact it was not because that excellent penitentiary had gardens and play yards and attractive facilities. The inmates of the prison were working on embroidery, making rattan furniture, sculpting and doing many other things for gain. Everyone in the institution was being paid. Some of the prisoners were receiving psychiatric care. The time within which prisoners were released was dependent in part on the money that they had earned and their attitude of mind as they prepared to go out to meet society.
I believe that incarceration is sometimes good. I have before me a letter from a minimum security institution written by a once successful professional man who did an evil thing. In this letter to me he says:
It is a strange thing to say, but I am happy that I have spent this time in prison. I have rediscovered myself, my family and life.
His wife, Grace, has written a very touching letter, much of which tells how this experience of humiliation and separation has redeemed their life together and given the family new hope. Although much has been destroyed, on the basis of this hope much can be rebuilt.
May 18, 1967

I think that as we desire and search as a people for a better country and the good society, we all must become deeply involved. Industry has not cared nearly enough about the penitentiary services of Canada. In some respects it has impeded progress. Organized labour has not cared nearly enough about our penitentiary services, and in some respects has impeded the rehabilitation and restoration to society of people who have offended. Our service clubs should be challenged to participate fully in this program, just as industry and labour should become a mighty industrial partnership to ensure that something better is provided.
I would leave with the house some of the thoughts of George Scott, a psychiatrist in the Kingston complex. He envisions a community which he calls "reward city" where people are moved progressively from maximum to medium to minimum security, until finally we have the open community where people work hard and live under free conditions and with good pay, developing their skills and attitudes of self-care and responsibility. Perhaps industries will compete one with another to establish plants in such rehabilitive communities.

In taking part in the debate on the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, my first words, of course, must be of commendation of the high quality of debate in this chamber during the last few days. I would be remiss if I did not comment on the efforts of the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. C6te) who started the debate.
Many interesting subjects have been covered but probably more time has been devoted to a discussion of constitutional matters and the streamlining of the procedures of this house than to any other subject. For my part I do not feel qualified to discuss either of these subjects, though I am quite sure that lack of qualifications and knowledge of a subject does not always rule out participation.
Reference was made in the throne speech to housing. I listened with intense interest to the remarks of the minister who is in charge of housing when he spoke in this chamber last week. I was particularly concerned to see whether there was to be a change in government policy toward alleviating what has been
The Address-Mr. McCutcheon referred to in the house as the crisis in housing. Apparently not, though the minister did state in reply to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) on orders of the day on Friday that his remarks contained very interesting material.
While I have the greatest personal admiration and respect for the minister, I cannot agree that there was much in his remarks to lend hope to the many people who are alarmed at the housing situation. Really what the minister said in essence was: "Everything will be O.K., everything will work out, if we just let the money lenders get more out of mortgages."
An increase in the mortgage interest rate may be essential, Mr. Speaker, but it is not the whole answer to the housing crisis. I feel sure that the minister realizes this as well as the other members of the house. The minister referred to his meetings across Canada this winter and reported on some of his findings in these words, which are to be found on page 93 of Hansard for May 11:
-the greater part of the criticisms was not directed toward what the federal government was attempting to do and was doing in this field.
The minister admits that criticism exists but he sidesteps responsibility, saying in effect that other levels of government are to blame. Nobody likes to take the blame, and it is very comforting to attempt to place blame somewhere else. However I suggest it is up to us all in the federal government to provide more leadership in the matter, and we should be more actively engaged in efforts to lower the price of houses and of mortgage money -both equally essential. There ought to be more money at lower rates.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Were the minister in the house I would suggest to him that merely to sidestep the responsibility, as he appears to be doing is not the answer. We ought to be conducting research into streamlining building procedures-and when I talk of building procedures I refer to all phases of the industry, ranging from financing into research into new materials.
The minister also said that we have maintained a good average of housing starts and completions over a period of years, and this I do not deny. It is easy for one to rise in his place and be critical, just for the sake of being critical, but that is not my intention. I hope to be constructively critical, and I hope to draw attention to the inadequacy of the
376	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. McCutcheon housing starts. I want to make certain suggestions, which I think are important for lowering the cost of housing.
A review of what has recently taken place in the housing industry might be helpful to understanding the problem better. This, briefly, is what happened last year and the year before that. In 1966 there were 134,474 starts, while in 1965 there were 162,192. In April the minister suggested in parliament that with an increased flow of mortgage money 155,000 starts might be made this year. He revised that figure in May and suggested that 160,000 houses would probably be started. Even that figure is 10,000 units short of the requirements as submitted by the Economic Council, which asks for 170,000 new housing starts for each year of this decade, and up to 200,000 yearly starts in the next decade.
Many things happened in 1966 to depress the building business, and here I wish to quote further statistics. Private lenders reduced mortgage loans. For example the trust companies reduced their loans by 48 per cent, the insurance companies by 31 per cent. The loan companies were down by 32 per cent. All lending was reduced from $2.5 billion to $1.6 billion, a reduction of $.9 billion. In an effort to alleviate the situation C.M.H.C. advances, taken from the consolidated revenue fund, were increased from $3.25 billion to $4 billion. This increased lending did not inject as much into the housing industry as was necessary. C.M.H.C. gave direct loans on 35,567 units; the private sector of the house building industry must have accounted therefore for 98,807 out of the 134,474 units started.
The life companies, on a dollarwise basis, disbursed more money in 1966 than in 1965, despite a marked decline for these companies in mortgage payments. Dollarwise and volumewise their business was up, but on a per unit basis it was down, serving to show how costs have accelerated. For example, in 1962, we see that 3.4 per cent of National Housing Act homes cost over $20,000; in 1966, the figures show that 27.5 per cent of National Housing Act homes cost over $20,000. I shall say more about that later, but at the moment I am particularly interested-

speechtext:
Yes. It is also irrelevant, as my colleague says.
As I was saying-and I expect the hon. member for Middlesex East knows about as much about housing costs as I know-costs for housing in 1966 increased at a greater rate than incomes and wages increased-taking into account even the Pearson 30 per cent formula for wage settlements. Here we see history repeating itself. In 1956-57 when costs advanced more quickly than incomes, we had a similar situation. In the year 1956-57 as in 1966-67 a Liberal government was in power, and I doubt whether these similar situations occurred through coincidence. It seems to me that here emphasis has again been put on the wrong priorities and no regard has been paid to the pocketbook of the little fellow who desperately needs a house.
In 1966 construction costs, per square foot for bungalows averaged $12.56. The increase over the year 1965 was from 8.1 per cent to 12.4 per cent, depending on location, and this compares-to answer my hon. friend's question indirectly-with an average annual increase of 1.4 per cent only for the ten years 1956 to 1966. Just think of it-costs rose in one year by as much as they had risen in the previous six years. In all fairness these increased costs cannot all be blamed on the government; nevertheless because of its lack of enlightened planning it has contributed toward this increase. Almost everything that has been done in housing has been done to take the easy way out.
I talked before of the increased C.M.H.C. ceiling, and I must mention in fairness that legislation was brought in last year providing for national housing money for older homes. The government also changed the ratio for calculating rental housing loans to 90 per cent of lending value from 85 per cent of lending value. This is not enough, certainly, "to excite the daring". A borrower needs 5 per cent less down payment, but the price of the house has increased by 8.1 per cent. That is not much of a gain, and the poor borrower is obligated for a bigger mortgage, and probably for a longer period.
I shall now speak of what the government did not do. It did not call more than just the organizational meeting of the committee of
May 18. 1967	COMMONS
this house on housing. There was one meeting, after which the committee was promptly disbanded because the government had not sent it a single thing to do.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Now a few words on the subject of the cost of money. The extent to which money and the cost of money affect the cost of residential accommodation is not often realized. Virtually all single family dwellings and apartment buildings in our metropolitan area, and indeed in every area are mortgaged in value to an extent ranging from 70 to 85 per cent. For every $10,000 of mortgage amortized over 30 years at the National Housing Act rate of per cent, the debtor pays back $24,300. In other words, he pays back almost two and a half times as much in total as the original debt. While there has been a great deal said in the past six months about how tight money is and how more money should be made avail-ble, there is not enough being said about the cost of this money and its effect on the cost of residential accommodation.
A loan of $10,000 amortized at 7J per cent over 30 years carries exactly the same debt service as $11,100 over the same period amortized at 6i per cent. In other words, the one per cent increase in interest costs has had the same effect as an increase in building costs of 11 per cent. We must bear in mind that buildings available be for rent or sale today were, for the most part, mortgaged prior to the time of these higher interest rates, enabling us to say that the present cost of housing accommodation does not yet reflect the higher cost of money which has occurred within the past year. This added cost must be borne by the renting or buying public in the months ahead, and must of course support the proposition that costs have not yet reached a peak but will continue to rise due to this pressure.
The federal government, I believe, can assist the mortgage market to a very marked degree. The present policy of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to tie the National Housing Act rate to the long term yield of Dominion of Canada bonds. To the extent that this policy, recently adopted, induces a greater flow of mortgage money to the residential mortgage market, it is a good policy. I cannot, however, accept the principle that a 1J per cent differential between the National Housing Act rate and Dominion of Canada bonds is reasonable, bearing in mind that the security of both is identical. The major difference between a government-guaranteed National Housing Act mortgage
DEBATES	377
The Address-Mr. McCutcheon and a Dominion of Canada bond lies in the liquidity of the investment and in its cost of administration. I believe that the federal government can, through C.M.H.C. or its subsidiary, incorporate and operate a mortgage bank for the trading of mortgages. While it may be too much to expect that the future will see a National Housing Act mortgage being traded over the counter with the same kind of movement and price that exists today with a Dominion of Canada bond, I believe that substantial narrowing of this differential can be obtained with reasonable market conditions.
If trading in mortgage money were to operate on almost an over-the-counter basis, as is the case with the bonds, the construction industry could plan for much longer periods at a time. This would mean a great improvement in efficiency as well as lower money costs and I firmly believe this is one way-indeed, it may be the only way-in which we can make the best of a bad situation. The construction industry admits to its own inefficiency of operation in many instances; but while admitting that improvements could be made, it quickly points out that the present method of financing each year's operation after a mad scramble each spring for funds is one of the main causes of present difficulties. Those directly concerned do not know whether they have enough money to operate for a year, so their employees are faced with lay-offs. And they do not know how much work will be available next year.
The government tried the $500 winter incentive plan, which obviously failed to work. I think the answer to improved efficiency in the construction industry, hopefully with lower costs, will be found by making a regular, planned flow of mortgage money available and allotting it over a longer period than is now the case, when only a season to season supply or forecast is available.
This may be the case-if the government does not decide in its wisdom on a tight money supply for next year or the latter part of the present year. There are many "ifs". I maintain that planning in all its phases, including financing, should be on a two to five year basis. Housing should not bear the brunt of any artificial tinkering with a supply of funds for the industry. House mortgage funds should not be used to dampen a business cycle or to accelerate one. There should be a steady flow based only on demand.
Regardless of any so-called lack of criticism of the federal government as reported by the
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. McCutcheon minister, only the federal government has the facilities to be able to envision a nationwide situation. Provinces and municipalities just cannot have this type of over-all perception.
In my opinion we missed a golden opportunity to rationalize our house building requirements when in our haste to implement the Canada Pension Plan we let the funding of the plan slip through our fingers, as it were, and allowed the provinces first claim on the assets.
This fund, which we are aware is only short lived, could have provided the massive injection our housing industry required on a temporary basis, that is to say, until we got caught up. Then in an orderly fashion the mortgage bank concept could have taken over. What a tremendous incentive it would be. How in keeping with a security program, that the funds collected under the pension plan could be used to provide homes for the population-the same homes, in many cases, which would shelter pensioners in their old age.
Another area of great concern is the tremendous cost of legal fees in connection with almost every house or property transaction. Time is money, and too often there are almost interminable delays in conveyancing. Naturally, delays can be very expensive. I do not think we can afford this luxury much longer and unless some streamlining can be achieved the system of land titles will have to be overhauled.
I think the provision of title insurance should be examined to see whether reasonable reductions in cost could be obtained by this method. The lawyer members of this chamber may not agree.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It is my opinion that lot sizes can and should be reduced. Through arbitrarily fixing minimum standards for lot sizes, in Canada we have added miles and miles of sewers, pavements and other services, so much so that our municipalities cannot stand the costs of servicing land for development. It does not matter who was responsible for these things in the first place. It seems to me that now each government level says, "This is not our department. We cannot do anything about it." Surely it is time we quit passing the buck. We are all in this mess together, all levels of government, and the thing to do is to pull together to get us out of it.
I suggest that it is just as important, yes more important, to Canadians to have the price of housing lowered as it is to have the

moneylenders back in the business at a very high rate of interest. With this in mind I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp)-and possibly since he is not in the chamber now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) will convey the message to him -that he should have another look at the tax on building materials.
Much has been heard about removing this tax. I am not suggesting that. I am suggesting something else, a relocation of it. I presume that the government will find it necessary to continue collecting this tax. You do not forget $180 million just overnight, but I submit to the minister that this tax should apply at the retail level rather than at the manufacturer's level. Why should Canadians have to pay a percentage profit markup on a federal tax at every level of business-first the jobber, then the wholesaler, then the retailer? This tax by the time it hits the consumer has been marked up at least 50 per cent, and then in most of the provinces we add on a sales tax.
I would suggest that the Minister of Finance give some thought to relocating this tax. I think he could automatically reduce it by 50 per cent and the government would not be out anything, but it would be very helpful towards lowering the price of housing. In summary, Mr. Speaker, if the relocation and reduction of the tax were accomplished, if the construction industry could be encouraged to improve efficiency by a few percentage points through long range government planning, with a reduction in mortgage rates obtained-and believe me, Mr. Speaker, all these things are possible-then a 10 per cent reduction in housing costs would be quite possible and no better project could be envisaged for this the centennial parliament.
