speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with my colleagues, and other hon. members, I wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Their speeches were not only a credit to themselves but a credit to Canada.
As a backbencher I have many grievances and frustrations but I am not going to dwell on them today. I am going to speak on something that I think is very important not only to Canada but to the entire world. On reading the speech from the throne, which I was not privileged to hear, I was struck by this one paragraph that deals with natural resources:
The great natural resources that we take into our second century will be vital to us in meeting
May 18. 1967

our needs and in maintaining our position as a major world trader. Measures will be introduced by the government at the present session arising out of the need to conserve and preserve the great wealth with which Canada has been so richly endowed.
Now Mr. Speaker, I thoroughly agree with the foregoing. Canada to my mind is not only one of the richest but the richest country in the world, richest in resources and in her people. But I notice one great natural resource with which Canada is endowed from coast to coast but which apparently is being neglected. As Canadians we are adopting an attitude toward this resource which not only will affect Canada greatly in the future but will affect the entire world. The resource to which I refer is gold.
Since before history was written gold has played a great part in the development of mankind, not only in the monetary field but in the fields of the arts and industry. We know that the people of Mesopotamia were working in gold more than 5,000 years ago. Their gold vases have been unearthed in Iraq, dating back to 3,500 B.C. Their workmanship showed that these goldsmiths knew the skills of working and shaping the precious metal.
At one time gold was Canada's foremost metal and brought in more money to Canada than any other metal. It is still greatly used as a commodity in the arts and in industry, and was the backbone of our monetary system up until a few years ago. I am not speaking of gold as one interested especially in gold mines but as one who has been in world trade for the last 45 years. The companies with which I have been associated were generally doing business with more countries than are at present exhibiting at Expo '67. I have found out that when tariffs were raised, when quotas were put into effect and other obstacles raised to world trade it was the lack of gold, or its equivalent, which was the cause.
Before the first world war Britain acted as the world's banker and all settlements of world trade were made in London. Britain was a free trade nation. She had currencies of all nations generally surplus to her own requirements, and it needed very little gold to resolve any balance of payments. The surpluses which Britain did not require were invested in other countries. No one at that time gave much thought to central banks or central bank reserves, as we did not seem to have any balance of payments problems. World trade kept moving along on an even keel, and increasing.

The Address-Mr. A. M. A. McLean
However, after the first world war Britain had lost at least $50 billion in her overseas investments and she could no longer act as banker to the world. As the United States was then the most financially powerful nation, she inherited the role that Britain had played for over 100 years. But the United States was a high tariff country and would not receive the products of other nations as payment for their debts. Consequently, the United States gradually stripped the world of gold and the nations of the world were forced off the gold standard. The various countries of the world had no common denominator on which to base their currencies, and so there was chaos in world trade. This caused a falling of prices and brought on world depression.
In 1934 the late President Roosevelt raised the price of gold from $20.63 per ounce to $35 per ounce, and in the legislation there was permission for a further raise to $50 per ounce, but this legislation was allowed to lapse in the United States as it had a time limit. The world then had in the American dollar a common denominator on which to base its currencies. There was an immediate increase in world trade, profitable prices were restored and we saw the lifting of the depression that had held the world in its grip for many years.
The rise in the price of gold not only revived Canada's gold mines but created many new ones, and gold became our foremost earning metal. It brought into circulation an enormous amount of gold which various peoples of the world had been holding because they distrusted the paper currencies of the world, thus making world reserves at that time adequate for the world trade that was carried on.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In 1945 the United States, along with the United Kingdom, was anxious to get a multilateral agreement with reference to monetary affairs. The result was the Bretton Woods agreement and the establishment of the international monetary fund, to which all nations joining contributed a definite amount of their currency backed by a 25 per cent gold deposit, and obtained certain drawing rights on the fund's balances. The United States agreed to buy and sell gold at $35 per ounce, and every nation signing the agreement agreed not to pay more than $35 per ounce for gold even if it was mined in their own countries.
Canada was the third largest gold producer in the world, and according to the Governor of the Bank of Canada and also the chairman
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. A. M. A. McLean of the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States, gold is a monetary measure. Then if we agreed to a fixed price, we sold our sovereignty; not internally, because gold does not affect the issue of currency in Canada, but it does radically affect the settlement of external balances.
If gold is a monetary measure, as the Governor of the Bank of Canada states, it should have the same purchasing power in 1967 as it had in 1945. But it is agreed by all economists that the purchasing power of the American dollar is down to 44 cents. Then the gold dollar should shrink to 44 cents in gold content. But I am also advised by no less an authority than the Governor of the Bank of Canada that gold is a commodity. If we are in a free enterprise country, the price of no commodity should be fixed in Canada by a foreign country.
The $35 per ounce for gold that is being paid by the United States today is not sacred. When the United States treasury pledged that the price of gold would not be raised by the United States, they were not speaking for the United States alone but for the entire world, and they were saying something that was just impossible. The price of gold is a world problem, not a United States problem. At the present time, with the American dollar depreciated to 44 cents, we are asking our gold mines to accept $15 or $16 per ounce for gold. This is an impossible situation.
If it was my voice alone that was raised you might ask: What does he know about the world financial situation? But I would repeat the words of Sir Roy Harrod, the economist who was consulted at the time the International Monetary Fund was formed, who advocates the doubling of the price of gold as a preliminary to the reorganization of the International Monetary Fund and the establishment of a new unit for world settlement-just as a preliminary. He states:
I regard gold as a sheet anchor of liberty- so it has been for many hundreds of years of civilization.
This is not only the opinion of Sir Roy Harrod; it is also the opinion of another noted economist, Sir Ralph Hawtrey, who stated that "gold is an anonymous asset." It is also the opinion of Jacques Rueff, a French economist. Sir Roy Harrod states that the International Monetary Fund should be reorganized with greater flexibility. Under present conditions certain nations have their currencies designated as reserve currencies, that

is, the pound and the dollar which are supposed to be on an equal basis with gold. These currencies are not sufficient for the reserves needed to keep world trade flowing smoothly and increasing. At the present time, although the United Kingdom quota to the International Monetary Fund is $2,450 million, the United Kingdom has borrowed through drawing rights $2,410.6 million. The United States gold quota to the fund is $1,290 million, and the United States has borrowed in gold from the fund $905.2 million. So it is quite apparent that the nations whose reserve currencies are supposed to finance world trade are the principal borrowers from the International Monetary Fund.
We certainly need a new international unit of settlement to help finance our world trade, for when the United Kingdom and the United States try to resolve their balance of payments problems by withdrawing pounds and dollars from circulation, they are simply drawing the sinews of world trade that are supposed to be financing it. All this is related to the position of gold, and gold is certainly one of our great natural resources in this country, which commodity the two eminent economists I have mentioned state should be doubled in price before creating a new international unit of settlement.
The First National Bank of New York, which is quite well known, especially to those of us who were members of the finance committee, states in its May magazine issue:
Lifting the gold reserve requirement for domestic note circulation does not mean that the United States could dispense with gold internationally. Even with all its productive capacity to give real value to money, the United States, as an international banker, requires a strong gold reserve. Foreign governments and central banks holding large dollar deposits and other short term assets in the United States, are fully aware of the intrinsic strength of the U.S. economy as well as of the fact that the dollar has, throughout the years, lost less of its purchasing power than any other major currency. Nevertheless, they expect us to maintain a suitable gold stock to provide what in their eyes is an assurance that the dollar will remain at all times a reliable and freely usable currency.
Yet people all over the world are holding billions of dollars of gold which they consider to be worth more than what the United States is paying for gold at the present time. If the price of gold was raised to what it should be, the United States would have no balance of payments problems; there would be free movement of capital around the world and there would be no inflation because other currencies would be adjusted to the gold
May 18, 1967	COMMONS
price, the same as in 1934. There would be plenty of liquidity, which is needed to finance world trade.
I am not interested in gold mines, as I stated before, but the very life of the companies with which I have been associated practically all my life depends on world trade. World trade in 1947 amounted to $48,549 million. In 1965-world trade amounted to $164,700 million. The reserves and liquidity that were adequate in 1947 are certainly not adequate today. Last year, with $2 billion worth of gold mined and put into circulation, not one dollar went into the central banks to finance world trade-it simply disappeared. The previous year, of the nearly $2 billion worth of gold that was mined, only $250 million got into the central banks. So no matter what the bankers think or say, the people of the world think that gold is the backbone of the financial system and a store of value. We have that opinion confirmed by the First National City Bank of New York.
Canada is one of the nations among the so-called Big Ten who are supposed to bring forth a realistic policy to solve the present monetary situation so that world trade can move smoothly, and increase. But I have watched the press in vain for the voice of Canada in relation to an increase in the price of gold, which to my mind and that of many world economists would be the first, preliminary step in solving our present international financial situation. I might say that the United States seems to have a closed mind on Viet Nam and a closed mind on the gold situation, for I addressed a letter to the Christian Science Monitor, which they refused to print, and I also addressed a letter to the New York Times which they refused to print, simply because they said their government would not agree with the policy.

The feeble excuse that a rise in the price of gold would benefit only Russia and South Africa is certainly not valid, for the western world produces three times as much gold as Russia, and if there were any benefit to accrue, three times as much benefit would accrue to the western world as would accrue to Russia.

The Address-Mr. Coates [DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If Russia were given increased purchasing power she would buy a great deal more of our products, and this fact is evidenced by the wheat purchase paid for in gold. Russia is not bound by the international monetary fund and she is allowed to put any value she wants on the gold produced in Russia. She can put a price of $35 an ounce or $75 an ounce and still put it into international currency. In this way Russia would have this extra purchasing power and this would be of great benefit to our industries in the western world.
South Africa in the same way could use her extra purchasing power to diversify her economy and would then be buying machinery of all kinds from the western world. Her Bantu population, which now has the highest standard of living in Africa, would certainly benefit through increased wages from a rise in the price of gold.

In entering this debate on the throne speech I must first of all say there is little in it to give Canadians the kind of confidence one would hope would be installed in their minds as we enter upon the second century of nationhood. I had hoped this speech would be inspirational, and one which historians could look back upon as an indication that Canada entered its second hundred years with inspiration for the continuing development of a better nation. I had hoped the speech would be one that would always be remembered by Canadians as the great turning point of this nation's history in the development of unity and purpose. Instead it reminded me of what a housewife might prepare for a light supper, much like what we in Nova Scotia have always called plain simple hash.
Everything in this speech has been talked about, dropped and then revived. It could almost be referred to as garbage except for those few things which will probably be of some benefit to someone. It certainly contains nothing inspirational. I am afraid that Canada will end up her first hundred years in the red, just as we have ended up consistently at the end of each year for the past ten years. The total sum of Canada's deficit from the fiscal year 1957-58 to 1966-67 amounted to $3,908 million. We are no longer spending our own
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Coates money, we are spending our children's money. I have one little boy who will soon be 12 and a little girl who will soon be 10, and in my opinion we in this parliament are doing a mighty poor job as administrators and guardians on their behalf. By the look of the estimates for the coming year we will probably end up with another deficit for 1967-68, and will have to tax the people to a greater extent than ever before. This seems both alarming and ridiculous.
Our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) keep telling us that things are great, that this country is moving forward, that investment is at an all time high and that the business community is confident. At the same time this government is allowing its cabinet ministers to spend more money than is being received in revenue. It is continually interfering in the affairs of the people of this country to a greater degree than ever before, by spending the taxpayer's money, when it should be allowing the taxpayers to spend it as they see fit. How much longer can we live in this fools paradise?
We were told that the fiscal year 1966-67 was one of the greatest years in Canada's history, that the economy was booming, and that there was more employment than ever before; yet this government committed the Canadian taxpayer to $230 million more than will be received in federal revenues. This was a time when the government should have been allowing the private sector of the economy to maintain the buoyancy, and a time when it should not have been meddling in the affairs of the public. I do not know how much longer Canadians are going to allow the government to press forward with legislation for the benefit to 10 per cent of the population, paid for by 90 per cent.
We must create a spirit of initiative on the part of the people and we are not going to do so by continually giving them everything they ask for without asking them to do any work. We should wake up to this fact, and wake up to it very quickly. I have no argument with deficit financing or with social justice, but I do suggest that neither is good if the result is national bankruptcy. Surely it must be becoming more evident to us that we are living far beyond our means.

For a period of time after 1957, we had to put more money into the economy because of a period of recession. According to some we came out of that recession in 1961, and according to others, in 1962. Surely we should expect from the government enough responsibility to leave individual freedoms alone when there is no reason to be meddling around with them.
From time to time I am impressed by the concern which the Canadian people have voiced from time to time about the fact that parliament is debating certain subjects for long periods of time. These people ask: Why do you not get on with the work and be more businesslike? I often reply to them that they do not know how lucky they are, that parliament has long debates on some subjects, because when parliament is being efficient and passing legislation it is doing one of two things: it is either passing a piece of legislation which infringes on and limits a citizen's freedom, or it is passing a piece of legislation which will cost the taxpayer more money. So the more time parliament spends debating these subjects, the less time it spends dreaming up new plans, and the better off the taxpayers are.
However, what we can expect and what we get from the government are two different things, and this is very evident today, as it has been in recent years. But what we as members of parliament have to do is to realize the heavy burden we are placing on people who have to foot the bill for the legislation we are passing. If it were only the taxpayers of today whom we were asking to carry this very heavy burden it would not be so bad, but as long as we keep running up deficit after deficit we do not stop with the people who are paying taxes today but are saying to the taxpayers of tomorrow: You will have to pay for the things we thought the country should have, for the things that we want but cannot afford. I am tired of

doing this, unless it is absolutely necessary or unless we are in a period of recession.
While I am not committed to any of the leadership aspirants who are putting their names forward at the present time, I think that Senator Wallace McCutcheon at least talked good common sense when he laid down what he thinks a political party should be doing in this day and age. Mr. Speaker, first I wish to join with those who have already spoken and offer my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Being selected to move or second the motion for the
DEBATES	385
The Address-Mr. Stefanson address is a personal honour which also brings honour to the people whom they were elected to represent. This being Canada's centennial year, Canada's 100th birthday, one cannot help but take a brief look at our country's past history and achievements.
When Canada entered confederation there were roughly five million people in this land. In the intervening 100 years, Canada's population has quadrupled and the population is now roughly 20 million people. One hundred years ago the vote on the bill to establish confederation was taken at 4.15 in the morning. The confederation bill was carried, 91 votes to 33. When we concluded the first session of the twenty seventh parliament two weeks ago, it was 3.20 in the morning. It would appear therefore that the parliamentary system is still functioning in much the same manner.
I am sure no one will deny that Sir John A. Macdonald was the architect of this nation. The meetings that were held at Charlottetown laid the ground for confederation, and these have been recorded in the annals of history. The dreams of Macdonald, Cartier and the other fathers of confederation started to take shape after the passing of the confederation act. Sir John A. Macdonald became Canada's first prime minister and his vision of a great confederation, guided by a strong national government, started to take shape. Under his leadership and wise counselling Canada, as a nation, got off on the right track. His dream of building one nation, a united nation from sea to sea, became a reality. Macdonald's task was not an easy one, nor has the task of succeeding prime ministers been easy. The road was never perfect; potholes always develop that need care and attention.
During the past 100 years, Canada has matured and is today recognized as a country of peace and good will. Today, Canada is a nation built of a strong moral fibre, a nation highly respected around the globe. As I mentioned before, the road is not always smooth. Potholes have developed, and these need care and attention. Sometimes the reason for the development of these potholes is unknown, while in other cases the cause is very real.
I believe all of us need to rededicate ourselves to the concept of one nation and national unity. Personally, I felt that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) set up a royal commission on bilingualism and bicultural-ism, he made a mistake. This should never have been done. I have not changed my view in this regard. I firmly believe this is the
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Stefanson cause of the development of some of the potholes. Most people were aware that some problems did exist, particularly between the two founding races. After the appointment of this commission, these problems became magnified and a divisiveness the like of which I have never seen before was created in this country.
This commission on biculturalism and bilingualism will not only be the most expensive commission in Canada's history, costing the people millions of dollars, but will bring about no solution to the problem. In fact I venture to guess that when this commission report that report will be put in a pigeonhole and left there. There were other ways of dealing with this problem. I feel that the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), that of convening a conference of government, of all political parties and representatives of all classes of society, to discuss the amendment and revision of the constitution, the bringing of the constitution back to Canada and the clarification and restating of our aims and objectives, was sensible and sound. This indeed would be a worth-while centennial project.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Canadians everywhere need to take stock of themselves and dedicate themselves to being Canadians first. There should not be any French Canadian, German Canadian, Ukrainian Canadian, Irish Canadian, Icelandic Canadian, and so on. I am not saying that one should forget one's racial and cultural background. I feel that everyone should be proud of his racial and cultural background, that one should use that background to become a better Canadian and a Canadian first. Then we would have Canadians of French descent, Canadians of German descent, Canadians of Ukrainian descent, Canadians of Irish descent and Canadians of Icelandic descent. In my opinion this type of attitude would help to make Canada a stronger and more united nation.
As a Canadian of Icelandic descent I suggest that each one of us, in this centennial year, dedicate ourselves to being a Canadian first, thereby helping to strengthen and unite our nation. This would be a good centennial project. I believe that people right across Canada are now in the mood to participate in the celebration of our country's one hundredth birthday. I think a lot of credit is due to our centennial commissioner, Mr. John Fisher, for radiating this centennial spirit among our people. I have heard Mr. Fisher
fMr. Stefanson.]
on radio and television, and read his articles in the newspapers urging all Canadians to join in and participate in Canada's centennial celebrations. I believe that Mr. Fisher is going to achieve the goal which he set and he deserves the whole-hearted support of all public minded citizens in bringing this about.
Expo at Montreal will be the biggest centennial event in Canada. It was when the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was prime minister that the world fair was awarded to Canada and the site of the fair chosen. The present government, when they took office, carried on with this project. All those who have been connected with this project deserve a lot of praise and credit, as there is no doubt that this will be the largest world fair ever. It will truly be a magnificent event, and something that should make all of us proud to be Canadians.
Another major event taking place this year is the Pan-American games scheduled for Winnipeg from July 23 to August 6. It was also when the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was prime minister that the pan-American games were awarded to Canada, and the site chosen. All those who are connected with the planning and staging of those games deserve a lot of praise and credit. The indications are that the entries for the pan-American games will be the largest in history and that they will also be the most successful. This will be another event that all Canadians can be proud of. I should like to mention here that the pan-American yachting or sailing races will take place on lake Winnipeg, near my home town of Gimli, Manitoba. That I suggest would be a good time for anyone travelling west this year to visit Winnipeg and take a sidetrip to Gimli.
Throughout the Selkirk constituency many centennial projects have been undertaken, including the building of skating rinks, curling rinks, community centres, parks, libraries and others. From this list one can see that lasting structures will be erected in many communities. Committees in charge of annual events throughout the various communities in the Selkirk constituency are going all out to make them bigger and better than ever before. Centennial committees have been set up in most communities and these are staging a variety of events through the year. The people of the Interlake area have caught on to the centennial spirit. This is a good year for people to pay a visit to the various communities in that area.
May 18, 1367

I wish to mention that the town of Selkirk is holding a fair and regatta from July 1 to July 9, and that the guests of honour will be Lord and Lady Selkirk. Also, during the Icelandic celebrations to take place at Gimli on July 31, the committee will have His Excellency, Asgeir Asgeirsson, the president of the Republic of Iceland, as its guest. He will also visit Winnipeg and Selkirk.
The speech from the throne was one of the longest on record but it was lacking in specifics. It dealt in generalities and hope. This is not good enough, when our nation is embarking on our second century. Most of the editorials which I have read have expressed disappointment with the throne speech, which consists mostly of words without substance.
What has happened to the 10,000 annual university scholarships promised by the Liberals in 1962, 1963, 1965-and promised here, in the house, in 1966? Education should be high on the list of priorities. Even though education comes within the jurisdiction of provincial governments, it has become abundantly clear that provincial governments cannot foot the bill for secondary schools, universities, technical schools, and the like. It is therefore necessary that the federal government share in the cost in order that our young people will be adequately trained. There is no mention of education in the throne speech, except a brief reference to the need for strengthening the adult retraining program.
This government has seen fit to discard the vocational and technical school program which was brought in by the Conservative government and which proved so successful. The federal government should sit down with the provincial governments to work out a cost sharing arrangement for education which would assure all our people of the fullest opportunity to acquire the best education and training possible. After all, our human resources are the most important resources in our country.
There is reference in the throne speech to the further reform of parliamentary procedure. Several members have already dealt with this subject. The member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) delivered what I considered an excellent speech on this topic. Personally, I do not think there is anything seriously wrong with our system. Freedom of speech and the freedom of the individual are
The Address-Mr. Stefanson freedoms that have to be guarded and maintained. When a parliament lasts over a year, as the last one did, the chances are that there is mismanagement, or that the government is being unrealistic in the amount of legislation it proposes. I believe that both of these were contributing factors in making the last session the longest in our parliamentary history.
The only reason parliament has to meet every year is to pass supply; its second function is to deal with legislation. The government has to gauge the amount of legislation to bring forth that can be dealt with in the time available. It is a mistake to have a session of parliament go over a year. The last session should have ended just before Christmas and the new session should have started in January, instead of in May.
The Prime Minister must be very careful in the choice of a house leader. The government house leader has one of the most onerous and toughest jobs in the House of Commons. One must possess many skills and virtues to become successful in this post. The Prime Minister, for the success of his government and indeed for the success of parliament, has to produce such a man. I do not know whether the newly appointed house leader has these qualifications. On his past performance in the house, it is very doubtful if he has; however, the challenge is his, and he may alter his ways and rise to the occasion-and I hope he does.
Another important factor is for members to discipline themselves and at times to practise restraint. I think this is more important than any rule change. Some of the vociferous members of this house should take stock of themselves and ask themselves whether, if every member took up as much time as they do, a session could ever be concluded. Some of these vociferous members are advocating rule changes and limitation of debate. Their motto seems to be that it is all right to deny other members the opportunity or right to speak, so long as they have their say. Here again it is self discipline and self restraint that is required.
With a government house leader who has good understanding and is capable of good management, and with properly disciplined members there would be no need for rules to curtail debates. Much more could be achieved by co-operation and agreement among members than by any rigid rule changes.
May I call it six o'clock?
May 18, 1967

When the house rose at six o'clock I had made a few brief comments about the work of parliament itself. The Montreal Gazette of May 10, 1967, carried an editorial the heading of which read: "Yearlong Session Here To Stay". I think this is an assumption which is accepted by all parliamentarians. What we do object to are sessions extending beyond one year. The article outlines means by which the business of the house could be handled in a more orderly fashion. It states that the estimates should be brought down early in the session. I have always believed that parliament should deal first with estimates and then with legislation and that the work of parliament would be done in a more orderly and efficient way if this practice were followed.
The article goes on to advocate fixed adjournment periods for the Christmas, Easter and summer recesses. I do not think anyone would quarrel with that suggestion. I wish to

quote briefly from this article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette:
No government should overload parliament and then publicly complain that its measures are not being passed. One of the advantages of a well-programmed year-long format is that experience would show just about how much legislation may reasonably be presented for parliament's consideration. As one session would almost immediately follow another, there would be no serious need to press too much into any one session. The reality of year-long parliamentary session is being imposed on practices and customs that grew up when sessions lasted a few months only. Reality and practice have still a long way to go before they can be brought into alignment.
This government has complained a great deal about our failure to pass various measures, and then in the next breath it brags about the amount of legislation which has been dealt with. If the government did less complaining and concentrated upon better planning and management of our sessions it would help restore the image of parliament.
Perhaps I should say a word about the former leader of the house, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith). I feel he was a good house leader and that he had many good qualities. He understood the House of Commons, and this is essential. But he made one mistake; he allowed the session to run beyond 12 months. This is intolerable and must not happen again. I repeat, for the benefit of the new house leader, that no session in the future must ever run beyond 12 months; sessions should be so organized that they invariably end within the 12 month period.
I have always felt that my first duty as a member of parliament was to my constituency. I therefore intend to touch on some matters which are of direct concern to my constituents, though no doubt they are of importance to people in other parts of Canada as well.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
First, I wish to make a brief comment about the sales tax on drugs. I am not so naive as to say that the government's revenue can be cut. Therefore by cutting out a certain tax one would need to find other means of revenue. I believe that the sales tax on drugs is unjust, unfair and downright discriminatory and that it should be abolished forthwith. Chambers of commerce in my constituency have promoted resolutions to this effect, and a resolution of this kind was passed at the annual meeting of the Manitoba Chamber of Commerce.
May 18, 19B7	COMMONS
The special committee on drugs has recommended that the sales tax on drugs be abolished. In reality this sales tax is a sales tax on sickness and on those who are sick. I sincerely hope that the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will see fit to act swiftly and remove this tax, because there must be a fairer and more just way for the government to raise the revenue it needs.
Now I want to deal briefly with water pollution. The throne speech makes reference to a Canada water act to combat pollution. At the present time one does not know what form this measure will take. It is abundantly clear that steps are needed to combat water pollution. Plans will be required to prevent further pollution of our rivers and lakes, and a definite plan has to be developed to clean up pollution in the rivers and lakes already polluted, and I think this includes most of the rivers in Canada.
To clean up the pollution in some of the rivers is going to be a massive job. The only government action to date is the amendment assented to on December 2, 1960, Part VI-B of the National Housing Act, which provides for loans for municipal sewage treatment projects. This section also provides for a 25 per cent forgiveness.
This act has been made use of by many towns, cities and villages, and a good start has been made to prevent further pollution, and also a start made to clean up existing pollution. However, much more needs to be done because the pollution problem is large. To make a thorough and successful job of combatting water pollution will require the co-operation and participation of all levels of government, of industry, of business, and the people themselves. I am happy to note that the government plans action to combat water pollution.
Next I wish to deal very briefly with national housing and the housing situation. In the throne speech there is reference to a special study of urban development. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), who reports for Central Mortgage and Housing, has held symposia on housing and urban renewal in conjunction with provincial governments. These symposia have been held in every province of Canada. I have attended two of these symposia or conferences in Winnipeg, and one at Selkirk. I would think that from these conferences many of the problems facing urban communities are known to provincial and federal authorities and the time has come for action to be taken, and not just for 27053-26

No doubt one could hold continual studies and keep on learning, but in my humble opinion the need for action and for plans to be put into effect to attack these problems is greater than the need for further studies which will only delay action.
The government and the minister in charge know that there is a desperate need for houses in Canada. They also know that the cost of houses is getting too high. Therefore the sales tax on building materials should be removed. Land price is getting excessive, and municipal taxes are getting too high. Action needs to be taken on these problems. If action is forthcoming on these matters it would encourage our young people to become homeowners. I believe it is important in our social way of life that a large portion of our adult population become homeowners. In this centennial year further studies are not the answer; it is action that is needed.
In the speech from the throne there is also reference to new incentives to promote industry in the north. I welcome anything that the government proposes to do to assist industry in northern Canada, and I can think of no better way to help promote industry in the north than to provide the necessary services such as roads and communications. I therefore would like to see the government renew the roads to resources program, which was of such great benefit, to help open up new territories in every province of Canada. I urge the government to renew the roads to resources program without delay.
Some time ago the government made a very grandiose announcement about convening a conference of ministers of highways to discuss highway policy for Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am happy first of all to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The mover, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) displayed a rare eloquence. As for the seconder, the hon. member for Nico-let-Yamaska (Mr. Cote), the Quebec farmers rightly see in him a true farmer who, in a simple and sincere way, has ably expressed his views on rural life in eastern Canada.
During these few minutes when I will have the privilege of giving my impressions on the speech from the throne, I will endeavour to speak at some length of regional and interregional development, within the framework of our confederative system.
According to some of our usual critics, there were few surprises in the speech from the throne. Would it be that those critics have forgotten the tremendous legislation and numerous achievements of the government in the first session of the 27th parliament, the longest in the history of Canada and one of the most productive if not the most productive? In this second session, Canadians expect the government to continue and consolidate the task already begun.
On May 11 last, in this house, the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked what had happened to the war on poverty, whether an armistice had been signed. Still, the last speech from the throne proves that the government is still fighting against poverty.
Indeed, what about the measures it will take to create an increasingly favourable climate for industrial development and the multiplication of employment opportunities?
What about the other measures he proposes in order to promote regional development, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, to help Canadians who must travel to find a job, to make manpower centres more effective, to develop the adult retraining program?
What can be said about those measures except that they concretize a war strategy on poverty, so that every Canadian may enjoy life and be increasingly happy in his respective province, in Canada?
Is it not one of the reasons why the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was able to state, further on in his speech: "We can be proud of our country's achievements." In my opinion, he could have said just as well: We can be proud of our country's achievements under the leadership of our present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
In addition to the numerous proposals-I counted at least thirty-there is what the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) called a lot of fuzziness and nonsense. In my opinion, it was more than normal, after a hundred years of confederation, for the government to draw up a summary of the last hundred years and to outline a program for the hundred years to come. It did precisely that by making a historic review and stating the basic principles underlying Canada as it stands today at the beginning of the second century of confederation.
I think that most citizens of my riding share those few impressions on the speech from the throne, because they are in accordance with their hopes to achieve economic stability for their region and to progress at the same rate as the other regions of Canada.
-the main considerations involved in achieving regionally balanced development in Canada, consistent with our other national economic goals,-
And here I quote the Economic Council of Canada.
The Economic Council of Canada, as well as several other government and private institutions, mentioned them on various occasions. The council and I quote:
-noted, first, the importance of reducing the relative disparities in average levels of income as they presently exist among the regions; and second, the need to assure that each region contributes to total national output, and to the sustained, long-run growth of that output, on the basis of the fullest and most efficient use of the human and material resources available to the region.

The Address-Mr. Guy LeBlanc
The riding of Rimouski is part of the pilot 'area in which was applied the development program of the Eastern Quebec Development Board published on June 30, 1966. That plan is an ARDA project which cost $3,849,000, at least 50 per cent of which was paid by the federal government. It proposes long-term development objectives to 1982 and shortterm objectives between 1966 and 1972.
At present, the problems to solve is that of the agency responsible for implementing the plan. According to E.Q.D.B., it is a matter of
-identifying the agency responsible for the so-called implementation stage of the development logic which presided over the relationship established between the various programs and projects.
The organization of that agency is the problem that is of concern and particular interest to the people at the present time. In the meantime, other provinces receive through ARDA several millions of dollars to develop their territory.
* (8:30 p.m.)
For instance, the readers of a Rimouski weekly, L'Echo du Bas-St-Laurent, were informed last January 23 that $89,250,000, including $62,136,000 from the federal government, had been spent to implement the rural development program in the northeastern part of New Brunswick.
What we want is an efficient structure of consultation and pressure. As far as the implementation is concerned, we want the procedure to be determined in the spirit of our democratic traditions, in the respect of the freedom of each citizen. We are confident that the government of our province will assume its responsibilities in this field and co-operate with the federal government in the implementation of the plan.
According to an account of the visit of the Quebec minister of agriculture to Mont-Joli, published in the newspaper Le Soleil last January 13, the minister intends to set up this organization, appoint a committee of the legislature and name a regional co-ordinator.
In any event, we would like the federal government to maintain its present serious interest in this matter and appoint its own official, whatever his title, to co-ordinate the various services of the federal government with regard to the implementation of the program.
Therefore, the statement made by the hon. Minister of Forestry and Rural Development

(Mr. Sauve) on April 24 last, was a little reassuring, when he said:
It will be our pleasure before the fall, to sign an agreement which will be a feather in the cap of both the provincial and the federal governments involved.
My constituents from Rimouski were right, I think, to be skeptical, apprehensive and to fear being involved in an unfortunate experience, doomed to failure. Some past experiences can illustrate the reason for that frame of mind.
About 40 years ago, large numbers of pioneers who intended to be farmers were led into the forest hinterland.
In the framework of a colonizing policy, they cleared the land and toiled hard. Today, their children leave them for the big cities, and they remain alone on land which has not fulfilled past promises.
Here is another example: At Pointe-au-Pere, a municipality quite close to Rimouski, was located for many years the piloting station on the St. Lawrence river which kept, among other things, the economic activity of the municipality balanced.
At the time of the Conservative government after 1957, our friends in the opposition agreed to the removal of this piloting station without apparently thinking of the economy of the municipality.
Before 1957, the Liberal government of the time considered the possibility of improving the wharf at Pointe-au-Pere which could have been the home port of a ferry capable of serving both shores the year round.
At that time, service was supplied almost ten months a year by an old and well-established company which had already taken steps to build a powerful ferry capable of year-round service.
In August 1961-
And I am quoting from the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1964:
-the Treasury Board gave approval in principle to the granting of a subsidy.
This subsidy was a capital subsidy which proved to be an amount of $2,363,650, that is the purchase price of the ship, including taxes and it was owned by a newly-formed company, other than the one whose plans were prepared under the direction of another company. I continue the quotation:
But in doing so, they emphasized that it considered a service of this nature to be primarily a provincial responsibility. The board was prepared
May 18, 1967

to make an exception in this particular case however, because it was in hand and other active consideration before the board recommended to cabinet a report on federal assistance to a ferry and coastal services under the principles of which intra-provincial ferry services that are essentially highway links-chiefly services involving roll-on/ roll-off ferries, are considered to be a matter of provincial responsibility.
Why did the Conservative government of the time arrange for the total capital subsidy to finally reach $2,363,650 so as to pay the full cost of a ferry without taking serious precautions for the future? Why did they agree with the company on a contract for only five years, terminating on December 31, 1966. Why did they not order a careful inquiry by their economists to make sure that the ship would be economic?
These are the questions my electors are asking now that they know the ferry was sold some days ago to British Columbia Ferries-according to the newspaper Le Soleil of May 6-for $1,850,000.
I think the present Liberal government would be sympathetic as concerns this ferry; but since then, the problem has become the exclusive responsibility of the provincial government. That is why the population will have to start from scratch and ask the Quebec government for help in reorganizing this service.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Another fact is connected with the maintenance of the port of Rimouski, that is the wharves of Rimouski-Est and Pointe-au-Pere.
For many years the port of Rimouski was the most important port of the Lower St. Lawrence, east of Quebec even from the Bay of Chaleurs up to Dalhousie inclusive. Since, some ports of the north shore such as Baie Comeau and Sept-Iles have certainly surpassed it during those last years.
One has only to consider the net amount of wharfage dues collected during the past five financial years to realize it; Sept-Iles, $480,000; Rimouski, $337,000; Dalhousie, $122,000; Baie-Comeau, $113,000; Forestville, $109,000; Chandler, $101,000; Sandy Beach, $79,000; Riviere-du-Loup, $38,000; Mont-Louis, $30000; Matane, $26,000; Havre-St-Pierre, $20,000; Ste-Anne-des-Monts, $17,000.
This can be explained if one considers that Mont-Joli, Rimouski, Price and the surrounding municipalities, with a total population of some 60,000 inhabitants, also constitute the largest group of the lower St. Lawrence and
The Address-Mr. Guy LeBlanc the gulf, and includes the greates number of public services.
Now, before the advent of the Conservative regime in 1957, there was, according to my information, a permanent staff in the field for the maintenance of these wharves.
Under the Conservative government, the system was changed and wharf maintenance people were dismissed and never replaced. Ever since, everything that should be checked yearly and regularly on these wharves is in a pitiful state.
Therefore the population is relying upon the co-operation of the civil service and of the present government to make the necessary improvements.
Facts of this nature spread some doubts in the people's minds. That is why they bank so much on the implementation of the recommendations of the development plan without which they may be doomed irrevocably.
Naturally, there are several other problems to be solved. For instance, what I said about the maintenance of the wharf at Rimouski could also apply to Trois-Pistoles.
There is also the organisation of the Canadian National Railways in our area. We hope to make, in the near future, to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) representations based on concrete facts and figures.
We also have a magnificent airport at Mont-Joli that was built during the last war for military purposes. It cost $3,059,491, which includes $1,735,019 spent on the construction of three runways. Improvements have since been made amounting to $695,030, which gives a total cost of $3,754,521.
Considering the difficulties of air transportation in the pilot territory, we are building great hopes on that airport in our efforts to develop the district.
In my area, as well as in the whole surrounding territory, agriculture has taken on the form of a familiar and current problem.
I think that our farmers, as well as those interested in agriculture, would like to make marginal lands fully economic, to gear production to ecological, climatic and economic conditions and to relate activities from one area to another, with regard to relations with the north shore of the St. Lawrence river and an industrialized agriculture. Our agriculture must remain a comparatively important activity.
In our area, positive action must be taken primarily at the very root of agriculture and
394	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Alkenbrack we must not rely solely on price control. Such a rationalization will enable farmers to obtain better prices for their products.
Manufacturing milk would seem best suited for intensive production on our farms; that is why I am always among those members who try to understand requests from our manufacturing milk producers and to bring the necessary pressure to bear in order to improve price conditions in this field.
Yesterday's vote-as all hon. members know-was not on the merit of the amendment; it was a vote of confidence in the government which, for many years, carried out a progressive program, on the whole, and accomplished more, particularly in the field of agriculture, namely with regard to the dairy policy, considering that a farmer who received $2.90 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk in 1963 now gets $4.75. That is why I voted with the government. At the same time I was convinced that I was voting in the farmers' interests.
A better balance in the area economic development in Canada is a most urgent goal to achieve. To that end, as we enter the second century of our confederation, the consideration of the necessary amendments to our constitution is certainly important.
Quebec wants, and rightly so, to keep its distinctive character as do other provinces.
Confronted with our American neighbour, Quebec considers it in its interest to remain within confederation, not only from the material and economic point of view, but also for philosophical, political and cultural reasons.
Remembering Lafontaine and Cartier, we still have reasons to continue to build harmoniously, a happy and flourishing Canada.
Therefore, at the beginning of this session of our centennial, with the achievement of an ideal balance between the regional sectors and a spirit of understanding among the provinces, we want to build a greater Canada, but just as serious-minded, just as daring but still always true to itself, always peaceful, so that we may be proud to say: We are Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not originally intended to take part in this particular debate, but lately matters pertaining to the record of the government and its effect upon the people have accumulated in my files. Therefore I rise to bring these matters to the attention of the house, hoping the government will take heed.
[Mr. LeBlanc (Rimouski) .1
DEBATES	May 18, 1987
Before I do so, I also wish to commend the mover and seconder of the address in reply, the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote). Both of these hon. members have brought a distinct honour to their constituencies. This brings to mind memories of the time in September 1962, almost five years ago, when I first came to this chamber, and the newly elected member for Nicolet-Yamaska, Hon. Clement Vincent, now minister of agriculture in the province of Quebec, had the honour of seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At that time the hon. member and I were roommates. We shared an office on the third floor of the west block. In the ensuing parliaments we were seatmates. I visited the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska many times as his guest, and he visited me in Prince Edward-Lennox.
He taught me French and I helped him with his English. This was to our mutual benefit. We were a working example, proving that Canadians of different races can get along together in harmony. We believed, and still believe, that all Canadians who respect each other's origin, social needs and geographical circumstances can live together harmoniously. The days are past when a narrow, provincial outlook regarding Canadian citizenship sufficed.
The speech from the throne asks for Canadian unity. This is why I must bring up a matter which does not make for Canadian unity, and which will demonstrate to hon. members the ignorant and narrow outlook of the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal and the discourteous and unCanadian treatment which they gave a 17 year old student from my constituency. The student's name is Mr. Jim Munro of Amherst-view, Ontario. As a result of this, his father, Mr. R. J. Munro, has written to me and asked me to bring this matter to the attention of the house. I will read the application for employment which the son made to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, as well as the reply he received. I will also read his father's letter to me. The following is the letter written by young Munro to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce:
Dear Sir:
I am writing to you regarding summer employment (June 10-September 1,	1967).
The reasons I am interested in obtaining work in Quebec are:
(1)	to broaden my speaking knowledge of French
(2)	to earn money to pay for my stay in Quebec and to save some money.
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Alkenbrack
I have taken four years of French in high school and have only a very basic knowledge of French. While I am unskilled and cannot speak fluent French, I realize extra hard work is an asset.
I am interested in finding out what your thoughts and recommendations would be in regard to:
(1)	type of employment available and corresponding wages
(2)	cost of living in the Montreal area.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Any information and/or assistance you may be able to supply me will be greatly appreciated.
Then, the Munro boy goes on to give his full name, address, his date of birth, his height, his weight, his education and his future plans. He says his future plans are to obtain high school graduation and enter university in a political science course. He closes his application with, "Yours truly, Jim Munro". The Montreal Chamber of Commerce did not even have the courtesy to write this young man a letter. They turned the letter over, put it in the typewriter and in capital letters with the red portion of the typewriter ribbon they typed across the back of Mr. Munro's application:
Sorry, no summer job available for non-Canadian.
La Chambre de Commerce du District de Montreal.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote the father's letter. You cannot blame Mr. Munro for being angry at such frustrating circumstances and the treatment of this ambitious young student. Mr. Munro writes to me from Box 167, Amherstview, Ontario, which is roughly ten miles west of Kingston. His letter reads:
Dear Mr. Alkenbrack:
We recently had something happen that upset and perturbed us very much.
Our oldest son, who will soon be eighteen, has been writing to the Chamber of Commerce of various cities requesting all pertinent information in regards to summer employment. In most cases, he has received a satisfactory answer.
In this group of cities was Montreal. The only acknowledgement received was his original letter back with these words typed in red on the back-
Sorry, no summer job available for non-Canadian. La Chambre de Commerce du District de Montreal.
The return address on their envelope is, Chamber de Commerce,
Du District De Montreal,
31 Ouest Rue St. Jacques Montreal,
How they have the audacity to classify him as a non-Canadian, we fail to understand.
To begin with, he was born in Ottawa while I was a member of the R.C.A.F. I served a total of over eight years during and after the war. I also had three brothers and one brother-in-law
in the armed forces during the war. My father in law was a veteran of the first world war but couldn't go in the last one because of medical reasons.
To top this off, my mother-
I am still quoting Mr. Munro, the father of this wronged student.
To top this oft, my mother is of French descent; also my father in law was born in the province of Quebec and moved to western Canada as a boy.
Since you are our federal representative, we feel that you should be the one to do something about this. Therefore, we would appreciate it if you would bring this ignorance to the attention of person or persons who will take action to straighten out such people.
Sincerely yours,
R. J. Munro
There is a notation that a copy was sent to Mayor Drapeau, Montreal. Now, Mr. Speaker, who is it in the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, "La Chambre de Commerce du District de Montreal" who is doing this? I am sure Mayor Drapeau does not condone it; I am positive of this. Whoever it is, they have been encouraged in their rudeness by this Pearson government because the Pearson policy of bilingualism and biculturalism has divided this country needlessly and nefariously, and to an alarming degree. This policy has encouraged just such cases of narrowness and ignorance as I have now brought to your attention. The Montreal Chamber of Commerce demonstrates, in this instance, that they discriminate against English speaking Canadians. They do not even recognize them to be Canadians because they answered Mr. Munro by saying he was not a Canadian. Of course, this case only illustrates the fact that when you discriminate against people because of their racial lines, such action quite often comes back to haunt you.
I say this because I have investigated this family. I find that Mr. Munro's grandmother, that is his father's mother, was Henrietta Bedard, a French Canadian girl from the province of Quebec. She bore a son who served his country in wartime in the R.C.A.F. for a total of over eight years. This noble French Canadian grandmother also bore three other sons who served in the armed forces during the war.
I have investigated the other side of the family tree and I find that the grandfather on the mother's side was a man named McGillvray of Thurso, Quebec. This family has been here since General Wolfe took Quebec in 1759; the family dates back to that time. I say to the government and to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce only this;
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Alkenbrack What a treacherous and despicable way to treat Jim Munroe, the grandson of this woman, just because he happens to live in Er-nestown Township in the County of Lennox in Ontario.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, just think what an adverse and unco-operative attitude this action will tend to create in the minds of our youth when they have been treated in this manner. I say to the Prime Minister stop encouraging this two nations policy. This case which I have brought to your attention is the result of this policy. Someone in the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, and I aim to find out who, has taken the Prime Minister literally and deduced as follows: The Liberal government in Ottawa says Quebec and its people have a special status under this Liberal, two nations concept, and therefore this person answered Mr. Munro by saying that there were no jobs there for non-Canadians. As I said before I intend to get to the bottom of this and I demand an explanation and apology to the Munro family by the Montreal Chamber of Commerce. I want the assistance of the government in doing so.
Now I must turn to the speech from the throne. This long discourse seems to me to be merely a rehash of promises made in the last four years. The government, as usual, has been non-productive of any useful legislation. I thought, and everyone noticed this, that they imposed on His Excellency the Governor General because, in many instances, he was forced to use flowery adjectives to describe alleged government action in the past or in the future. In short, Mr. Speaker, the government was covering up its careless and profligate actions of the past with words, words and more words. At times, and in some sections, the speech sounded like a lecture, not to parliament alone but to the Canadian people.
Nowhere in the speech was there any mention of economy by the government or of the great need that is upon us right now to reduce taxation in order to give people a chance to build homes and raise their families without going bankrupt. The government admits that inflation is rampant. It is beyond their control or they would do something about it. The latest cost of living index, standing around 148 for the month of April, is the highest in history. Last May 27, almost a year ago now, Mr. Speaker, I brought this matter of national importance to the attention of the house. My speech is recorded on page 5607 of Hansard and in it I referred to consumer credit, the cost of living and expressed some opinions concerning the Bank Act.

I am glad to see that some action has been taken in connection with the Bank Act along the lines I recommended. I commend the government for these new banking measures which are now in force and are of benefit across the country. These provisions give the chartered banks an opportunity to participate more fully and to compete for consumer credit. I notice that my words of last May 27 regarding money on deposit were prophetic because the chartered banks are now paying far more interest than formerly on savings accounts. This is a good thing, because it enables the little people who cannot afford to take a chance on the stock market or to buy bonds, to save money at a rate of interest which is at least as good as the yield on some bonds. What is more, Mr. Speaker, they save this money in their local bank.
c (9:00 p.m.)
I am sorry to see that nothing has been done about the plight of the consumer and the spiralling cost of living. True, the government is going to form another department and a minister has been named to head it. But this will only increase taxes, Mr. Speaker, which is part of the cost of living. This matter could have been dealt with without the formation of another department. I believe we now have 26 ministers of the crown. We must remember that the consumer has to pay for all of this extra expenditure. This will mean the building of another departmental empire in Ottawa. I suggest this matter could well have been handled by the present President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon). He is an economist and he is once again a member of the cabinet. He is also an authority on external affairs, though the Prime Minister no longer takes his advice.
No effort has been made, according to the speech from the throne, to take any measures to lower taxes or reduce the needless spending of millions of dollars. On the contrary, just as we started this new centennial session the government bought a $300,000 painting, the purchase of which has infuriated the majority of the people of this country. I would ask the members of the cabinet as well as my colleagues in the house to go and look at this thing in the art gallery, and then to take a journey around the country. In fact, one does not have to go very far from Ottawa into either Quebec or Ontario to see some of the poverty that exists.
We are now finding the ministers of this government apeing some of the sayings of our good neighbour to the south, when they talk
May 18, 1967

of Canadianism in terms of "the affluent society". This is a myth; there is no truth in it.
It is an insult to the intelligence of at least half the people of Canada.
I suggest that to move toward any form of affluence we must stop taxing the working man at the rate we are today. The working man is raising a family and trying to pay off the mortgage, as well as buying groceries, clothing and insurance. As a member of this chamber I think I can truthfully say I have always been one who tried to pay close attention to the fair and well founded opinions of the people. With regard to just one facet of this question of taxation I should like to quote a letter which I received from one of my constituents, a man who works in a plant and has to provide various accoutrements and tools to perform his job. He says:
Dear Sir:
A new safety ruling at my place of employment, effective 1st May, 1967, states that employees are required to wear safety footwear, or toe caps fitted over ordinary footwear. The toe caps are supplied by the company, but are very awkward to wear, so the only alternative is to buy, at our own expense, less a 25 per cent discount, paid by the company, our own safety shoes. This I did, at a cost to me of $12.98 plus 5 per cent sales tax. This set me to thinking and I have come up with the following suggestions that you, living in a working man's area, will probably agree with and may be able to bring to the attention of the authorities.
1.	All safety equipment purchased by an employee, should have the sales tax eliminated or an allowance for different work categories be set, to be deductible from federal income tax return.
I appreciate that he is talking about the 5 per cent provincial tax, which has nothing to do with us; but he is making some very worthy suggestions regarding deductions from federal income tax for some of these personal expenses, which do pertain to Federal powers and I agree with him. He goes on:
2.	All work clothes purchased by an employee should have the sales tax eliminated, or a clothing allowance be set, to be deductible from federal income tax return.
I would draw the attention of hon. members to the next suggestion because I know many of them have had it put to them:
3.	An employee driving to and from his place of residence to his place of employment, whether the employee uses a chartered service or personal vehicle, to have a transportation allowance set, to be deductible from federal income tax return.
4.	In the case of tradesmen having to purchase their own tools and equipment, an allowance be set, to be deductible from federal income tax return.
The Address-Mr. Alkenbrack
Do you think a signed petition would have any effect on the powers that be? Please advise.
Thank you.
Sincerely,
Donald A. Young
Mr. Young is from Amherstview, Ontario, and I totally agree with his suggestions. This account, put forward so ably, should be heeded by this government. The lack of exemption from tax on certain items is unfair to labourers of this category. Here is a place where the government could save some money for their taxpayers, at the same time creating better home conditions for their families by letting them use these tax exemptions to the benefit of their families. I would urge the government to give this matter their positive attention.
The speech from the throne also made reference to modern communication, and for this reason another matter that I wish to mention is mail service. Here I address my remarks to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). The mail service between Toronto and Picton and Toronto and Napanee is very poor and very slow. Many businessmen and professional people in both towns are being inconvenienced by the slowness of our so-called first class mail delivery. The other day in the Picton Gazette there was an article dealing with this poor service, and the headline which I thought quite amusing, suggested that the pony express might be faster. This is absolutely true, Mr. Speaker. We in Picton cannot receive a letter or mailed parcel from Toronto in less than two days. A letter or parcel also takes two days from Toronto to Napanee. Optometrists, dentists, doctors and businessmen who send small parcels back and forth to laboratories, government and business offices in Toronto cannot receive these mailed articles in less than two days, and sometimes it takes longer. Only the other day my secretary mailed my personal cheque to me at the end of the month to my home in Napanee, and it took four days for it to come from Ottawa.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I have had many complaints about this from both Napanee and Picton. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the pony express would be faster. I did some homework on this and discovered that in 1840 a man named William Weller, whose headquarters was in Prince Edward county and after whom Weller's Bay was named, an old-time stagecoach proprietor and driver, drove Governor General Lord Sydenham from Toronto to Montreal by stage and team of horses in 35 hours and 40 minutes.
May 18, 1967

repairs and changes in the Smiths Falls-Napanee line that it may become, as it originally was, the main route from Ottawa to Toronto, and points beyond. Great savings can be made.

I thank hon. members for their agreement. I had been saying that the shortest route between Ottawa and Toronto by rail is by way of Napanee. In this way-in the way I had spoken of-the railway could increase its intercity business, shorten travelling time, between Ottawa and Toronto, and increase its business at Napanee, which serves a large area for the railway. With the completion this summer of the Quinte skyway, seven miles west of Napanee-this is the new bridge across the bay of Quinte joining Hastings with Prince Edward county-the railway at Napanee ought to obtain additional business from Prince Edward county. Of course that depends on what service is available. I urge the railway to use this line, as it would bring the railway more revenue and provide the people with the service they need-and heaven only knows, dangerous highway traffic would be decreased as would be the death toll through accidents.

speechtext:
I am
rising to take part in this debate as one who has had a lifetime interest in the conservation and development of our human and national resources. However, first of all I must compliment the member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) on his eloquent and moving speech when he moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne, which I notice received repeated applause from all sides of the house.
The Address-Mr. Herridge As I listened to him speak with such knowledge, assurance and conviction, and heard his choice of words and phrases, do you know, Mr. Speaker, I had a vision that inclined me to believe he could have had some part in the composition of the throne speech. Furthermore I congratulate him on his courage to admit that he voted twice against becoming a Canadian, but now, after 18 years within confederation, that he would choose Canadian citizenship over that of any other country on earth. He is what might be termed a convert, as the result of his experience here.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I wish also to compliment the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on his well informed presentation of the problems of the rural community.
I was particularly interested in his plea to members of this house not to use the farmer as a political football. That is a very noble precept but I am afraid, after 22 years experience in this house, that the hon. member is underestimating the human frailty of members of parliament, who can be tempted on occasions to use any issue as a political issue.
I have known this to happen on two or three occasions in 22 years.
The contents of the speech from the throne provide some hope that the government intends to introduce legislation which will be of advantage to Canadian people as a whole and particularly to the advantage of our older people who require an adequate standard of living, of those who require housing, of our farmers who seek parity of income, and of young people who require education, and others who need retraining. Without doubt, in my opinion, the speech from the throne offers a great opportunity for the exercise of imagination on the part of members of the opposition.
I must say I was very disappointed that there was no reference in the speech to veterans affairs and no mention of proposals for amendments to legislation which would be of benefit to veterans and their dependants. In this connection I have solid support. I listened with great interest to the speech made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) who is the chairman of the standing committee on veterans affairs, a highly respected member of this house. I will not repeat what he said. I will merely say I endorse wholeheartedly what he said in this house on May 17 with respect to the omission of any reference to veterans affairs from the speech
May 18, 1967

The Address-Mr. Herridge from the throne. He went on to deal with the need for amendments to legislation which would provide higher incomes for pensioners and improved allowances for recipients of war veterans allowances. I also wish to endorse what he had to say about the Wood committee. I know some members are impatient about the time taken by that committee in making its report, but it has been very thorough in its study.
I must say that the chairman of the Wood committee is highly respected by veterans in this country. He and his colleagues have heard a great deal of evidence, some of it in recent weeks, and I am glad to know that they are giving such careful consideration to the representations made to them. I do not mind this committee taking a little extra time, because the veterans and their organizations are confident that it will present an excellent report when the time comes to bring it forward.
I notice one curious omission from the throne speech-the total absence of any item announcing the government's intention to establish in Canada the office of ombudsman. This was mentioned in the speech from the throne of 1965 and I trust it will be brought forward later after we have disposed of some of the more urgent legislation. I know that members of this group as well as of other parties in the house are of the opinion that a measure to set up this office should be introduced as soon as possible, because of the changing nature of our society, to protect the individual and his civil rights.
I was delighted with the paragraph referring to natural resources and pleased to note that measures will be introduced to preserve and conserve them. We look forward to the introduction of that legislation. I was also pleased to note that we shall be asked to approve a new Canada water act which will provide a framework for the improvement and implementation of a Canada water policy. Having said this, I think that in fairness to the people of Canada and to the members of this house the government should announce its order of business in the immediate future so as to give priority to the more pressing needs which concern the people of this country today.
I intend to deal with the conservation and development of our natural resources, in the firm conviction that we can only maintain and improve our standard of living if governments direct their attention to this question

now. There is no time for delay. I am not only expressing my personal views; I am speaking on behalf of large groups in this country which are deeply concerned about this subject-one which I have followed closely in this country, particularly during the last four or five years.
I also wish to deal with the present state of affairs as far as our natural resources are concerned and to indicate our failure to protect them in Canada to date. It may surprise you, Mr. Speaker, but 1 wish to direct your attention to the Columbia river treaty and to what has happened so far.
