Mr. Speaker, Canada is confronted with many economic problems; the methods of production are developing rapidly; our government must appropriate a greater share of its budget to the implementation of welfare measures. We live in a capitalistic system whose philosophy is outdated, and nobody seems to want to reconsider it. However, that study has already been made and I am a little surprised to see that it has not been a subject for study in this parliament.
It has appeared in two books entitled: Le Manifeste capitaliste and The New Capitalists of Louis-O. Kelso and Mortimer J. Adler. The New Capitalist has not yet been translated in French.
Several influential businessmen have popularized those theories and I think that their suggestions could be useful, to us also from the province of Quebec.
The Manifeste capitalist sets out the doctrinal and economic meaning of the basic principles of a just theory on capitalism, as conceived by the authors, Messrs. Kelso and Adler, and which leads to nothing less than a capitalist revolution.
Democracy in its political form cannot exist unless certain economic conditions are ideal for freedom and equality for all. Men cannot enjoy freedom in the political sphere if they are deprived of it in the economic sphere.
According to the authors, if the defenders of capitalism have shown that communism was the enemy of political freedom and equality, they have offered no practical program for a classless society based upon economic equality. They have not met the challenge of the communist revolution in suggesting a capitalist revolution which, by applying the true principles of capitalism, would establish the economic democracy we need as a basis for the political democracy.
According to Mr. Kelso's theory, capitalism, developing according to its very principles and without admixture of socialism, could create a free and classless society on which political democracy could be based and through which the institutions of a free society could be preserved.
This concept of capitalism is the only alternative to communism, for our partly socialist capitalism is an unstable mixture of principles. Provided one has some sense of justice or attachment to the democratic idea, one
DEBATES	405
The Address-Mr. Emard could not wish to revert to primitive socialism, according to Mr. Adler.
No mind with any sense of the scientific and industrial revolution which is hardly beginning and which will have transformed our society within one hundred years, could consider our partly capitalist and partly socialist economic system as a system capable of staying in balance between these two opposing forces.
One of these two forces is socialization and the reduction of rights of capital ownership. The other is the effort to preserve the traces of rights of capital ownership. If one gives in to the first of these forces, one is led to the socialist and the communist revolution. If the other force is accepted through the development of the full potential of the rights of private ownership of capital and through the establishment of a harmonious relationship between these rights and the principles of economic justice, one is led to the ideal situation which will be the result of the capitalist revolution.
The author believes that the capitalist revolution will bring to all men liberty as well as equality. It will make economic activity dependant upon political activity, and it will give the control of material riches to the government of man.
The capitalist manifesto does not proceed from a revolutionary party whose self-imposed duty is to overthrow the existing order. Quite to the contrary, its aim is to emphasize, in the present economic system, the reasons required to give it a new life and to find the basis of a better society wished by all.
Mr. Kelso wishes for a revolution within capitalism, because according to him, even though no baleful darkness is sweeping down upon America, all forms of socialism are coming in through the back door.
The author is wishing for a capitalist revolution and explains that unadulterated capitalism, that is, capitalism untinged with socialism, is the only economic system consistent with a democracy. Finally, he attempts to prove that we are very far from having such an economic system and that we do not have yet a clear concept of what that system should be. What is praised under the name of "capitalism of the people" is a mixture of capitalism and socialism. If the phenomenon of socialization continues to gain ground with the considerable technological improvements which have now become possible, we will move ever closer to socialism, that is state

socialism. Nothing can stop that movement forward unless it is a capitalist revolution.
That revolution is justified by the author in these terms, and I quote:
Industrial economy, that is capitalism, will always exist in one form or another. The industrial production o 1 wealth is an established fact in our economy. The same goes for the disappearance of classes in our society. What we may chose is the form these events will take. For we have a choice.
The totalitarian state, with its population of puppets, writes Mr. Kelso, is not the unavoidable form which a classless society can take, not any more than state capitalism is the unavoidable form that the industrial economy must adopt.
Having stated that capitalism must exist, the author adds that we must choose between three, and only three, solutions. But the choice boils down, in fact, to two possibilities, since it is quite unlikely that the people of the free world would want to exchange their way of life for that of Soviet Russia.
We can decide to perpetuate the mixed capitalism we created in the last twenty-five years, hoping that it will last in spite of the dangers inherent in it, or else we can get rid of the contradictory elements of that socialized economic system which slowly push it towards state capitalism. The principles of justice which would contribute to the development of pure capitalism would take their place. In other words, we must choose between the status quo and the capitalist revolution.
The need for a capitalist revolution should be obvious to all those who understand the principle of a just economy and who see that the constitution of such capitalist economy is essential to economic freedom and political democracy.
According to Mr. Kelso, it is right and unquestionable to say that capitalism is our only alternative. Such affirmation would be purely academic if a practical scheme could not be applied to arrive at the expected results. The idea that capitalism is the only appropriate structure for an industrial economy and the economic counterpart of democracy, deserves the sustained attention of the public only to the extent that academic truth can be matched with a practical scheme.
In his book, Mr. Kelso emphasizes in particular the measures intended to encourage a greater participation of the individual in capital investments. To the profit-sharing method which is widespread, according to him, the

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, April 21, and again on Wednesday, May 10, I put the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
In view of the request of the International Transport Workers Federation that jet air lines be prohibited from using JP4 because of the high inflammability of this fuel, is the minister considering taking steps to ban the use of this fuel by Canadian air lines?
In reply to my question, when I asked it on May 10, the Minister of Transport said that consideration was not being given to my request because, as he said, the opinion contained in my question was not supported by such scientific evidence as was available. I put the question down for one of these late shows because of the considerable public interest that I find there is in it, and because I felt a more extensive statement would be desirable.
Everyone knows that the efficiency of our air lines is at a very high level, and yet there are times when accidents do take place. When they do occur, there are occasions when the most serious result is from the fire that follows a crash. As I understand it, those who are interested in this matter feel that the possibility of such fires could be reduced if the fuel used by jet airliners were of lower inflammability than is the case with JP4, which I understand is used in Canada and is certainly used by our own air line, Air Canada.
The International Transport Workers Federation, to which I have referred in my question, set up a special committee to study this matter. That committee reported that JP4, which is 8 per cent cheaper than the paraffin used by most air lines, is far more dangerous, due to its high inflammability. I understand that only four of the world's airlines use it at present, namely Air Canada,
May 18. 1967

KLM, Sabena and Japan Airlines. I also understand that the use of JP4 has been banned in at least some countries.
The Minister of Transport referred the other day to scientific evidence. In other words I gather the matter has been given some study. But such evidence as I have indicates that the men who fly the planes, as represented by the study and the thinking of their organizations, are concerned.
I am sure that we all share with them the desire that the danger of fire following the crash of an airplane might be reduced to as low a point as possible. If the fuel that is being used by Air Canada today is less expensive than some other fuel, while one would hesitate to object to any attempt to economize, if by using a less expensive fuel we are running a greater risk, then it seems to me this is a poor policy. If there is any possibility at all of reducing this kind of risk, we should be all for it, and I hope that the parliamentary scretary who is going to answer for the minister tonight will indicate that this whole question will be given further study.
If there were any way to do so I should like to transfer the rest of my time to my colleague, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir), who has a very important question. But I know that I cannot do that. I trust I may now anticipate a hopeful answer from my hon. friend, the parliamentary secretary.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express through you to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the regrets of the Minister of Transport on his inability to be here tonight to answer this important question.
The answer to the question as to whether the government is considering banning the use of JP4 fuel can be put very simply. The brief answer is no. JP4 fuel, however, is frequently under study. There were extensive studies made right after the war into the inflammability of this jet engine fuel and its vulnerability in terms of explosiveness during crashes and incidents of that kind. It was decided then, and it has been decided on subsequent occasions, when the explosive nature of these alternative fuels has been under study, that JP4 fuel is as safe as any alternative fuel that can be used for jet engine purposes.
I have personally made a few inquiries this evening about the use of JP4 fuel. I was told
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that a number of air lines, in fact the majority of world airlines, use JP4 fuel. Under certain conditions it is safer than parafin, basically kerosene, which is used by some of the other air lines. On other occasions it is less safe. However, it is the total range of conditions which must be considered, particularly conditions under which jet aircraft fly in this country. In other words this situation has been reviewed carefully. It is being reviewed from time to time and will be reviewed again as new fuels are developed and as circumstances change.

speechtext:
On April 19, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) gave an answer to an hon. member on orders of the day with regard to additional health services. I am very pleased that the minister has done me the honour this evening of staying here for the late show to give me a further answer. The question the hon. gentleman asked was, in effect, what procedure is going to be used in providing additional health services by the provinces to the national health plan. In his reply the minister said, in part:
The method of adding further health services to the health plan has been set out in the bill. The attitude the government of Canada took at the conference-
That is the conference between provincial and federal authorities.
-was that when a consensus developed amongst the provinces as to the importance of further services, the government would consider adding those services to the plan.
His answer is a little longer than that, but that is the relevant part of it. Now, I believe we should take a look at the relevant clause in the bill. The minister will find there is nothing in that clause relating to a consensus of the provinces before further services can be added to the health plan. As a matter of fact, the relevant clause in the bill reads in part as follows:
In the application of this act to a plan established by an act of the legislature of a province, any health service of a kind prescribed by the minister to be required health services rendered by a person lawfully entitled to render such services .. . under such terms and conditions as may be specified by the governor in council-
As you will see, there is no reference there to a consensus and the reference is to the province, in the singular. It is evident that a
408	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournmnt Motion single province may, under an act of its legislature and of course in agreement with the minister and the governor in council, add any additional service.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
During committee study of this bill many opposition members asked the minister as to whether any single province could set up additional health services. There are too many questions of this sort to name this evening those who posed them, but as an example of the kind of question that was asked I would refer the minister to page 10765 of Hansard for December 6, 1966. An hon. member said:
I take it this means that the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, can extend paramedical services in a plan in a particular province even though other provinces have not asked for a similar extension. In other words, the minister would be free, under this amendment, to accede to the request of a particular province that wanted to add to the services which are provided under this legislation, and it would not have to wait until a majority or a specified number of provinces, indicated their desire to have these paramedical services included.
He ends by saying:
I hope the minister's interpretation is the same as my own, namely that any province will be able to go ahead with providing additional services, provided of course that the minister and the governor in council agree.
We in the opposition who supported an amendment on the strength of the minister's statement that any one of a number of provinces could make available additional health services are deeply concerned at the apparent reversal of government policy and the stand taken by the minister. We would expect the minister to reaffirm the undertaking that he gave to the committee at that time, that a general consensus of the provinces is not necessary to initiate additional health services.
I hope that the minister in his reply this evening will not repudiate the commitment that he made during the discussion of the bill, a commitment that was accepted in good faith by all members of the house. When the vote on an amendment to clause 4 (3), which is the relevant amendment, was taken it was supported by all members of the house, I think mainly because of the commitment that was made.

Mr. Speaker, there are really two aspects to the question raised by the hon. member. The first has to do with the amendment, which is a matter of 'aw. It is a

DEBATES	May 18, 1967
fact that the governor in council would have the authority under the amendment to make available additional services, and to make such services shareable under the medical care act, even if a single province added such a service to its provincial plan. That is a correct interpretation, and in my reply to the question that had been put in committee, which asked whether the government would be free under this amendment to accept additional services if provided by a single province only, I said it would, and that is the case. That is the question of law.
The policy has been unchanged from the beginning. It was set forth first by the Prime Minister, that any province on its own was free to add further services-and can still do so-but without any sharing feature. The Prime Minister went on to say that when a consensus developed among the provinces for the inclusion under the medical care program of any additional services, the government was prepared to consider any extensions. I made that clear in the course of the debate. I recall that I stated that the only recommendation that I expected to make and that I would make under the amendment that had been passed was with respect to certain surgical procedures performed in hospitals by dental surgeons.
My hon. friend's interpretation of the law is quite correct. I confirmed in committee that that capacity is conferred on the governor in council. The question of policy has to do with consensus. When a consensus develops among the provinces for the addition of further services, they will be considered by the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with the question I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), namely whether the minister was aware of the many complaints made against the military manoeuvres going on at the Bag-otville military base, during which airplanes break the sound barrier, thus causing real damage on farms and even in the cities. Everyone wonders why the Department of National Defence selected that part of the country to give free rein to the wild antics of certain pilots. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Lake St. John area, which is 80 per cent agricultural, was once very peaceful, and farmers lived there under a glorious sun.
May 18, 1967

Since the government established this notorious Bagotville base, the people, apart from living under a heap of clouds, are possessed with fear on account of the hedgehopping supersonic aircraft. Those planes startle dairy cows to the point of causing losses to their owners. The flyers' madness is such that they break the sound barrier, shattering windows all around.
Mr. Speaker, I suffered myself from that since the window panes in my store were shattered to pieces, which caused a great deal of damage.
You may say that we can lodge complaints, but just wait and see. As a matter of fact, once we are through answering their questions, they always find some way or another to tell us that the air force is not to blame and that the flyers never broke the sound barrier at such an hour, such a minute and such a second.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think we have numerous proofs of that and so as to give you an example I brought here a letter from a good farmer, it may not be written in perfect French, but I want to read it just the same, to show that what I am saying is true.
I hereby take the liberty of writing to you about something which aggrieves us in the Lake St. John area. There are thousands of us in the same boat. This is due to the fact that the jet planes from Bagotville fly over the region of Roberval making an infernal noise by flying at times at altitudes of 800 feet. When they exceed the speed of sound, there is such an explosion that the earth shakes, windows break, and livestock are so frightened that they pile up in corners, in pigsties, in hen-houses. We lose animals every day. Everybody is nervous and we are sick and tired of those infernal machines; we ask the hon. minister concerned to kindly do something about it.
Mr. Speaker, I see that the minister concerned is not here but we do have the honour of having with us the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), and I believe that this is also important from the point of view of health.
I wonder whether we will be forced to put up much longer with the actions of these lunatics who play with million-dollar toys paid with farmers' taxes.

There should be enough space in the uninhabited territories in northern Quebec to leave alone a farming area as the Lake St. John valley.
And what about the nuclear bombs and warheads which the government stored in Bagotville, despite the farmers' protests.
I, therefore, ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare, since the Minister of National Defence is not here and does not want to bother about it, to try to do something for the public health and free us from this nightmare which is the bane of our farmers. [English]

speechtext:
I regret that the Minister of National Defence is unavoidably absent this evening, but I have listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Roberval. I should like to reply to his question by saying that it is the practice of the Department of National Defence to conduct military manoeuvres away from the populated areas of Canada.
According to the information I have received, there has been no over-all increase in flying training exercises carried out from the Canadian Forces base at Bagotville. Both the authorities at Canadian Forces headquarters and the authorities at Canadian Forces base, Bagotville are unaware of any recent complaints from civilians in that area. Any complaints from the civilian population in the area receive the personal attention of the commanding officer of the base. Additionally, Canadian Forces headquarters is informed by a message and a letter outlining the complaint and the action that is proposed to be taken by base authorities.
I would suggest that the hon. member, who has given details with regard to incidents in the area, might, pursue the matter by direct contact with the commanding officer. Undoubtedly the Minister of National Defence will be examining the reports made and undoubtedly he will take some action.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
